title: What is the Budget and what could be in it?
content_c:
What is the Budget and what could be in it?
- Published
Chancellor John Healey will set out Labour's tax and spending plans when he delivers his first Budget on 28 October.
He has refused to rule out tax increases after acknowledging government borrowing costs are at "historic highs".
But the government's room for manoeuvre on tax is limited.
Before the 2024 general election, Labour promised not to increase three big revenue earners for the government: income tax, National Insurance and VAT.
What is the Budget?
In his statement, delivered to MPs in the House of Commons, Healey will set out how the government plans to raise or lower taxes.
Alongside the Budget, the Treasury will publish details about the measures and their costs.
The independent Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), which monitors government spending, will also publish an assessment of the health of the UK economy and a forecast of what it thinks will happen in the future.
What might be in the Budget?
The run-up to the Budget typically generates speculation about what might be in it, which the government is trying to keep to a minimum this year.
Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households and meet commitments on defence spending, while also sticking to Labour's manifesto commitments on tax and the government's self-imposed fiscal rules.
The previous chancellor, Rachel Reeves, set out two main rules, which the new leadership has vowed to follow. These are:
- Not to borrow to fund day-to-day public spending by the end of this parliament
- To get government debt falling as a share of national income by the end of this parliament
In March, the OBR calculated that the first rule would be met with a gap - or headroom - of £23.6bn. However, this headroom is expected to have shrunk.
Analysts are divided on how much it may have fallen by. While a rise in government borrowing costs will increase debt interest payments, higher inflation could push up tax revenues.
KPMG believes the government's buffer could have fallen to £12bn, but the Institute for Fiscal Studies estimates it could be £20bn.
There has been speculation over what specific measures will be announced in the Budget.
Bank taxes
Bank bosses have told the BBC they expect Healey to raise taxes on the sector. UK banks have been reporting bumper profits, leading to calls from unions for higher taxes.
The Treasury has options: it could raise a 3% surcharge on profits which was lowered from 8% under the previous Conservative government, or it could raise the bank levy that is based on the size of their balance sheets.
Your First Home scheme
Further details on the Your First Home scheme, aimed at helping first-time buyers in England to purchase a property, are expected to be announced in the Budget.
The scheme will allow people to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.
There were concerns raised that the threshold for eligibility for first-time buyers could be set at £90,000 for a combined income outside London, and £110,000 in the capital, which could have excluded couples such as teachers and nurses, or police officers.
But that threshold is will now be £110,000 outside of London, and £140,000 in the capital, the BBC understands.
Capital Gains Tax
There had been speculation that Capital Gains Tax (CGT) - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value - could be changed, through either higher rates or by removing or amending exemptions. However, this has now been ruled out.
Support for pensioners
Pensioners on low-incomes are expected to be shielded from income tax through a new personal allowance. The government had already committed to not taxing people who only get an income from the state pension. But the full state pension is set to rise above the current £12,570 threshold, meaning about one million people would have needed to pay tax.
Tax on businesses
The Times has reported, external that online retail giants such as Amazon and eBay are expected to be made responsible for collecting tax owed by traders using their platforms.
The paper said the money raised is expected to be used by the government to cut business rates for High Street shops, by raising the threshold at which small companies start paying rates from £12,000 to £18,000.
He is also planning support for small breweries.
Fuel duty
Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze, deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year.
Healey told the BBC in late September that the time and place for dealing with rising petrol and diesel costs was the Budget, but would not give details on whether the freeze would be extended again.
Energy bills
Household energy bills are set to see their biggest rise in four years in January, with a typical annual bill forecast to jump by £276.
There has been speculation, external that Healey is planning energy bill help for households on certain benefits.
Mansion tax
The High Value Council Tax Surcharge - dubbed the mansion tax - was announced in last year's Budget and will apply to properties in England valued above £2m from April 2028.
There had been speculation that the government was considering extending it to properties worth more than £1.5m. However, reports now suggest, external Healey has ruled this out.
Cutting red tape
Healey has said the government plans to slash "form-filling and pointless paperwork" to save UK businesses up to £800m.
Ministers have said the proposed changes in regulations will reduce unnecessary bureaucracy for businesses.
Social and affordable housing
Healey is expected to add another £1bn to the £39bn planned spend on social and affordable housing in England over the next decade.
Devolved spending
Regional bodies and mayors in England will be given greater powers over spending, starting with £285m next year for things like housing, transport and High Streets. In future the regions will be able to borrow to spend more on local priorities.
What are opposition parties saying?
Opposition parties have released their alternative budget proposals.
The Conservatives are urging the chancellor to reduce spending and borrowing, as well as to cut green taxes, red tape and benefits to bring down energy bills.
Reform UK are recommending that the chancellor adopts 60 policies which they claim will create jobs - including approving the controversial Rosebank oil field - a project Healey is understood to back.
How is the economy doing?
In the first three months of the year, the UK's economy grew by 0.6%, while in the April-to-June quarter it grew by 0.5%.
The most recent data showed the economy grew by 0.1% in August after growth of 0.4% in July, with both figures stronger than expected.
Analysts say the UK economy is proving resilient in the face of energy price shocks caused by the US-Israel war with Iran.
Energy prices jumped after the conflict led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil and gas trade.
Economists expect UK growth to slow in the months ahead as those costs continue to weigh on households and businesses.
Prices for goods and services are still rising faster than wanted. Inflation hit 3.1% in the year to August, the highest rate in five months and above the Bank of England's 2% target, driven by higher petrol and diesel prices.
The Bank of England held interest rates at 3.75% for the sixth time in a row in September, but said they were likely to rise if high energy prices persist.
What time is the Budget and what happens afterwards?
The Budget speech usually starts at about 12:30 UK time - after Prime Minister's Questions - and lasts about an hour.
It will be broadcast live on the BBC iPlayer and on the BBC News website.
The Leader of the Opposition, Conservative MP Kemi Badenoch, will respond to the speech in the House of Commons.
MPs debate the measures for four days, before voting on them.
If approved by MPs, tax changes can come into effect immediately.
However, the government must pass a finance bill to make them permanent.

MPs debate the measures for four days, before voting on them.
If approved by MPs, tax changes can come into effect immediately.
However, the government must pass a finance bill to make them permanent.

title: Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders
content_c:
When Xi Jinping came to power in 2012, he pledged to stamp out corruption all through the ranks of the Communist party. More than a decade later, the pace of investigations has not slowed. Last year, China’s disciplinary authorities opened investigations into more than 1 million people, including more than 100 officials at or above ministerial or provincial level.
As Chinese Communist party (CCP) officials kick off an important meeting this week, discipline – and party loyalty – is high on the agenda. For those who try to read the tea leaves of elite Chinese politics, concern about the apparent lack of discipline is dominating CCP discussions.
The “fifth plenum” began on Monday and is set to focus on “major issues on advancing the party’s full and rigorous self-governance”, according to a Chinese state media. In party-speak, “governance” is a byword for discipline, loyalty and anti-corruption.
As Xi continues to crack down on corruption, the fact that investigations nearly always result in a conviction begs the question over whether targets are truly guilty of corruption, or are they just political rivals to the people in charge.
Kerry Brown, director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London, explained that in Xi’s worldview, which is obsessed with discipline and loyalty, there may not be much difference between the two. “If you’re corrupt, you’re not politically loyal. If you’re politically loyal, you’re not corrupt,” Brown said.
He added that in the CCP system, “corruption is not just material things”, but also “spiritual corruption”, which includes political disloyalty.
Some analysts argue that the reason that the anti-graft drive is so enduring is because corruption is a feature rather than a bug of an authoritarian, top-down political system with a sprawling bureaucracy that governs 1.4 billion people.
Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, said: “Xi has made the party less corrupt and strengthened his control, but he knows that tougher punishment cannot fully resolve the problem of officials putting their own interests ahead of the party’s.
“Xi’s answer is to keep tightening discipline, making anti-corruption a permanent method of governing with no obvious point at which he can declare the job done,” Thomas said.
The job may be never ending, but the plenum is an opportunity to refocus the party’s energy on discipline. The fifth plenum is the fifth of seven gatherings that normally happen in every five-year cycle between CCP congresses. The plenums bring together more than 300 members of the CCP’s Central Committee, the most senior officials in the party hierarchy.
The meeting is particularly significant because it is likely to be the last substantive meeting before next year’s 21st Party Congress, where a new Central Committee will be chosen, and where Xi is expected to be anointed for a fourth term as the head of the CCP.
Eliminating anyone who poses a risk to his authority or to the party’s credibility is a key priority for Xi. And potential threats are everywhere. Nearly 15 years after Xi took office, according to CCP proclamations and a host of recent investigations, the problem is still not stamped out. “It is a deeply ingrained part of [Xi’s] worldview,” said Brown. “Everyone else is corrupt”.
In the past, Xi has warned that the party could “lose its ruling status and inevitably be eliminated by history” if it could not get its house in order. “This is by no means an exaggeration,” he said.
The current focus on party governance comes amid a host of high-profile investigations against senior party and military leaders.
In January, Zhang Youxia, China’s top general and a man second only to Xi in the military hierarchy, was placed under investigation; he was expelled from party last month, having already been removed from the military’s top ruling body, the Central Military Commission (CMC)
A host of other purges means that the CMC, which normally has seven members, has been reduced to just two: Xi and Zhang Shengmin, the CMC’s head of discipline.
Other recent scalps include Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang, and Huang Qifan, the former mayor of Chongqing.
Huang had long been known as the ultimate survivor in Chinese politics because of his connections to the scandals in the early 2010s in which Xi’s political rival, Bo Xilai, the former Party boss for Chongqing, was embroiled in the death of the British businessman Neil Heywood. Bo was ultimately convicted of bribery and embezzlement, for which he is serving a life sentence, but Huang survived. No longer.
Some China analysts have asked whether the recent purges, which have reached the highest echelons of the Party and military ranks, indicate instability in the regime. But Xi likely sees it differently. Corruption investigations demonstrate who is in charge. Plus, Brown added, they are “the most easy and natural tool by which to enforce unity and discipline”.

title: The boss whose twice-bust business appears to be back despite £3m debts
content_c:
For three decades, the recruitment industry treated Andrew Woosnam well.
Having learned his trade during the 1990s, he graduated to create his own firm at the turn of the millennium – which allowed him to bank millions of pounds in salary, dividends and loans and to buy assets including a grand house in Berkshire once owned by the comedians Dawn French and Lenny Henry.
But life has become much tougher of late for Woosnam, whose recruitment business has twice entered insolvency proceedings since September last year. His three-hectare (six-acre) property – which cost £2.2m in 2013 – is now being eyed by insolvency professionals chasing him on behalf of creditors owed more than £3m by his bust companies, including more than £1m due to the UK taxpayer.
This all represents a stark change in how Woosnam’s Premier Group Recruitment appeared just a few years ago, when it was trumpeting its status as an award-winning business.
Woosnam owned 99% of the shares in the company, which went into administration in September 2025 owing £2.9m, including £647,000 to HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC), who had begun enforcement proceedings against it.
The recruiter’s assets were acquired three days later by a new company, called PGGBR Ltd, also owned by Woosnam, who made an initial £10,000 payment and promised administrators he would transfer a further £600,000 via monthly £25,000 instalments over the subsequent two years.
Adding up the future promised payments meant Woosnam theoretically trumped the £321,000 of cash offered by a competing bidder for Premier’s assets, although his detractors might argue that this arrangement had all the hallmarks of a structure that has been criticised as being highly risky for creditors: pre-pack administrations. These can allow a connected party to buy back a business on a deferred consideration, and have been cited in a series of studies that appear to show they tend to result in worse outcomes.
So it transpired in the Woosnam case.
The payments he had promised from his phoenixed business failed to materialise, while the new company ran up a further £400,000 debt to HMRC, according to the latest Companies House filings. The Guardian approached one of the Premier Group joint administrators based at KRE Corporate Recovery but he did not return phone calls asking about the case.
Woosnam had received a £1.2m director’s loan from the defunct Premier Group and had taken dividends out of the company totalling almost £2m since 2022. He also appears to have received a further £200,000 via a director’s loan from PGGBR before the new phoenix company was placed into liquidation last month.
If that sounds terminal, there is a possibility you may have underestimated Woosnam, whose twice-bust business now appears to have resurfaced for a third time. While it is unclear if the businessman is behind the rebirth or not, at least eight of Premier Group’s former staff now say they are working for a new recruitment brand called Xpertis Talent, which was created in July 2026 and looks so much like the two insolvent Woosnam companies that even employees seem confused.
One Xpertis recruitment consultant, who previously worked for Premier Group, has attributed an industry award won by the original company in 2022 to the fresh venture in marketing materials posted on the professional networking site LinkedIn.
Another employee has posted on LinkedIn that he started working for the third company before it had even been registered with Companies House.
Woosnam, who did not respond to invitations to comment, is not a shareholder of the latest company, which Companies House filings show is wholly owned by an individual based in Thailand. Woosnam is understood to have Thai family, although it is unclear if they are connected to the new business.

title: Germany news: Fire flares up at Hitler's Eagle's Nest retreat
content_c:
Germany news: Fire flares up at Hitler's Eagle's Nest retreat
Published October 24, 2026last updated October 25, 2026
What you need to know
- A fire that has almost destroyed a retreat in the Bavarian Alps used by dictator Adolf Hitler flared up again overnight
- Most people in Germany believe the conservative-led coalition government will come to a premature end, a survey shows
- The German president presented a prestigious environmental prize
- Low-cost carrier Ryanair has followed through with its plan to close its base at Berlin's international airport
- Chancellor Friedrich Merz has addressed the Bavarian CSU party conference as the governing coalition faces high degree of dissatisfaction
This blog is now closed.
Read below for a roundup of stories making news in Germany for the weekend of October 24-25.
Thank you for reading
Thank you reading this weekend's Germany news blog.
We'll be back with a fresh blog tomorrow with more developments from the heart of Europe.
Stay tuned with DW.
Cruise ship and container ship collide in Bremerhaven
A cruise ship has collided with a container ship in the northern port city of Bremerhaven, police told the DPA news agency.
Tui Cruises confirmed the collision of Mein Schiff 3 in response to a DPA request.
The cruise ship had reportedly returned to the pier where the damage was being assessed.
There were no reports of injury.
Audi CEO's appearance at Trump rally described as a 'disgrace'
As a German reporter, suddenly seeing German CEO Gernot Döllner pop up in the middle of a Trump campaign speech in Perry, Georgia, was a particular surprise.
Publicly, German automakers have said they won't be blackmailed. But this was a clear transaction made under pressure.
Trump's remark on Audi's investment, that "without tariffs they would not have been coming in," left no doubt of his understanding of the "deal."
The crowd cheered the $4.2 billion (€3.8 billion) investment that Trump said will help create up to 30,000 jobs.
But the open instrumentalization of German business investments just days ahead of a US election is already ruffling feathers in Germany.
"A disgrace," said a lawmaker from the junior governing coalition partner SPD.
An "undignified spectacle," were the words used by the Handelsblatt daily business publication to describe it.
Fire flares up again overnight at Hitler's mountain retreat
A fire that broke out on Friday evening at the Eagle's Nest mountain retreat in southern Germany that was once used by Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler erupted again overnight to Sunday in the almost destroyed building, Bavarian police said.
A police officer said flames there burnt again at "room height" after smoldering embers provoked a flare-up in what the officer said was a common occurrence in the case of such conflagrations.
The renewed fire triggered another deployment of firefighters to the site, known as Kehlsteinhaus in German, at the top of the Obersalzberg mountain.
The site, formerly used by Hitler to receive diplomats and other foreign guests, has been a restaurant since 1952 but was closed on Friday when the fire broke out. No one was injured.
Police arrested a 33-year-old German man suspected of having lit the fire, with an initial psychiatric assessement indicating mental illness.
The building was largely destroyed by the blaze, which caused millions of euros of damage.
IN DEPTH: Audi defends decision to open plant in US
After US President Donald Trump on Saturday announced that car producer Audi would build a $4 billion (€3.77 billion) assembly plant in the state of Georgia, the company has defended its planned move against criticism that it goes against German interests.
"This decision was preceded by many months of careful planning and intense negotiations," CEO Gerbot Döllner told reporters on Sunday.
"If the American president invites you, you accept the invitation. That is what respect for the office and for the country in which we invest demands," he said, arguing that the plan could protect jobs in Germany by boosting the carmaker's global business.
The move is yet to be approved by the supervisory board of Volkswagen, which owns Audi.
You can read more here: Trump announces Audi will build $4 billion factory in US.
German Environmental Prize goes to climate-action lawyer and wastewater engineer
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has presented this year's prestigious German Environmental Prize, worth €500,000 ($560,150), to a lawyer specializing in environmental cases and an engineer who has developed high-performance filters for wastewater plants.
At a ceremony in the western city of Aachen, Steinmeier commended Hamburg-based lawyer Roda Verheyen and engineer Klaus Vossenkaul as models of environmental protection.
"They show that each and every individual can make a difference," he said.
According to the German Federal Environmental Foundation (DBU), which awards the prize, Verheyen received the honor for "getting justice done for the environment."
In his speech, Steinmeier said she had shown many people ways to fight for their interests amid human-induced climate change.
Among other things, he said, her constitutional complaint against the climate protection law in 2021 played a decisive role in the Constitutional Court's ruling that Germany should become climate-neutral by 2045.
Speaking about Vossenkaul, Steinmeier said the engineer was a prime example of "creativity and inventiveness" in the field of environmental protection.
The president said the membrane technology developed by Vossenkaul helped to make wastewater plants more economical in terms of space, energy and cost, thus protecting "our basis of life."
Most expect coalition government to fall before end of term — survey
Just one in four people in Germany (23%) believes that the coalition of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative bloc and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) will last its full term till the next federal elections at the start of 2029, a survey has shown.
Some 44% said they believed the coalition would end within the next two years, according to the YouGov survey of 2,202 eligible voters, while around 13% are even convinced that the coalition will not see out the year.
Conservative voters who support parties in the so-called Union — the alliance of Christian Democrats (CDU) and Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) — are less optimistic about the coalition's continued existence than SPD supporters.
A whole 53% of CDU/CSU voters expect a premature end to the coalition, compared with just 32% who think it will last out its term.
That compares with the 46% of SPD voters who doubt the coalition's long-term viability, with 34% trusting it will cohere until 2029.
Twenty percent gave no opinion on the issue.
The coalition has been divided over a reform of Germany's pension and welfare systems, as well as over the best way to deal with the challenge posed by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which beat the mainstream parties in recent state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Football: Bayern Munich coach Kompany to remain in hospital after collapse
Bayern Munich head coach Vincent Kompany is set to remain in hospital for several days and will be missing for a number of weeks after collapsing at the club's training center on Friday.
The 40-year-old Belgian had recently been suffering from a virus and collapsed while observing a reserve team training session.
"The good news is he's stable," said Bayern's director of sport, Max Eberl, on Saturday. "I spoke with him last night, and with his wife too. It wasn't a nice moment for any of us. He collapsed on the pitch yesterday and will spend a few more days in hospital until everything is checked over."
Eberl said that doctors are "trying to find out what it is," adding: "The tests have already yielded some results, but further results are needed to determine exactly what it is and how long it will take for him to recover."
Eberl said it will be a while before Kompany is fit to return to work. "We're not talking in terms of days, but weeks," he said. "We're all clear on that."
Kompany will miss Bayern's game away at high-flying SC Freiburg on Sunday, with assistant coach Aaron Danks set to stand in for him. He will also miss next week's Bundesliga Klassiker at home to Borussia Dortmund and the difficult trip to Atletico Madrid in the Champions League on November 3.
"It shows again that health is the most important thing in life, not football," said Eberl, stressing that Kompany will "only come back when he's fit."
Bayern will also travel to Freiburg on Sunday without captain Joshua Kimmich, whose father passed away aged 57 this week.
Goalkeeper Manuel Neuer will also miss the game due to "persistent tendonitis" in his foot, as will defender Min-jae Kim, playmaker Jamal Musiala and forward Luiz Diaz.
Ryanair closes base, cuts routes at Berlin's international airport
Low-cost Irish airline Ryanair has closed its base at Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER), and removed 12 routes there at the start of its winter timetable.
The move was announced in April and confirmed in October, with the airline having long complained about high taxes and fees at German airports.
Six of the 12 deleted routes, from BER to Palermo, Marseille, Triest, Reggio Calabria, Tallin and Pisa, can now no longer be directly reached on flights from the airport, the airline and the airport operator FBB said.
The other six — Gran Canaria, Fuerteventura, Lanzarote, Bologna, Thessaloniki and Vilnius — are served by other airlines flying from BER.
The seven Ryanair aircraft that were based at the BER airport have been reassigned to airports in European Union countries that, according to Ryanair, have got rid of aviation taxes or reduced airport charges.
Ryanair is to still fly to and from Berlin using planes based elsewhere.
The operators of BER have pointed out that despite Ryanair's move, eight more destinations can be reached from the airport than last winter, as other airlines have expanded their services at the airport.
  
Welcome back as we resume our Germany coverage
Guten Morgen from DW's newsroom in Bonn as we return to our reporting on the German stories currently hitting the headlines.
We will be looking again at developments as a fire at the Eagle's Nest mountain retreat in southern Germany once used by Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler flared up again overnight.
Meanwhile, a survey has shown that most people in Germany do not believe the current conservative/center-left coalition under Chancellor Friedrich Merz will last the full four-year course of its term.
And Europe's largest low-cost carrier, Ryanair, is closing its base at Berlin's international airport as previously announced, meaing that 50% of the carrier's flights there will be cut.
Read on here for more on stories from and about Germany.
We're pausing coverage today
We're pausing our coverage of the weekend's news out of Germany until later on Sunday morning.
Hope to see you then! Bis morgen früh!
WATCH: Hitler's mountaintop 'Eagle's Nest' goes up in flames
An overnight fire engulfed Eagle's Nest, a historic Nazi-era site once used by Adolf Hitler in Germany's Bavarian Alps. Firefighters faced difficult conditions battling the flames at the mountaintop location, while one suspect has been taken into temporary custody. Police are looking into whether this is a potential case of arson.
DW spoke to historian Sven Keller of the Obersalzberg Documentation Center about the site's historical significance, why it was preserved, and how Germany deals with landmarks associated with its Nazi past.
German national facing trial over alleged attempt to join 'Islamic Sate'
Germany's prosecutor's office said that a German national has been placed in pre-trial detention for allegedly attempting to join the so-called "Islamic State" terror group, while abroad, German news agency dpa reported.
The agency cited a spokeswoman for the Federal Prosecutor's Office as saying that an arrest warrant had been executed and that a 21-year-old was extradited to Germany.
The suspect is accused of travelling to Ethiopia from Berlin in January 2025, with the purpose of joining the IS terror group in Somalia and receive training there.
Prosecutors allege that he never reached Somalia, but instead traveled to Pakistan to join Islamic State, where he was reportedly arrrested in February 2025.
The suspect stands accused of attempted membership in a terrorist organization abroad. He is also accused of preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state.
Merz highlights threat from Russia
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz highlighted the threat Germany faces from extremist parties to foreign enemies, including a "massive threat" from Russia.
"How do we safeguard our freedom and our security in Europe, in the face of growing threats from extremists within and foreign powers from without?" the chancellor said, adding that Russia was seeking "to destabilise Germany on a daily basis."
Germany is one of the biggest military and political supporters of Ukraine and has been on high alert for acts of sabotage in recent months.
That's especially since an explosive-laden drone was discovered near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport. Berlin said Moscow was behind the attempted attack.
In one of the most recent incidents, on Thursday, police in the German state of Brandenburg arrested a Ukrainian man on suspicion of spying for Russia.
No change to 'firewall' when it comes to AfD, says Merz
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz once again stood firm on any notion of ever working with Germany's far-right.
Merx restated his opposition to any change in the"firewall" policy of isolating the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) at the CSU conference in Munich.
"Anyone who feels they have to vote for these people has no place in our Union. They have no place amongst us," Merz said.
The AfD, has been topping national opinion polls although a Friday poll showed Merz's conservative bloc closing the gap.
Nevertheless, according to the poll, Merz's coalition would still fall short of a majority were an election to be held.
The poll, conducted for public broadcaster ZDF, asked voters which party they would support if a federal election were held this Sunday.

The crowd cheered the $4.2 billion (€3.8 billion) investment that Trump said will help create up to 30,000 jobs.
But the open instrumentalization of German business investments just days ahead of a US election is already ruffling feathers in Germany.
"A disgrace," said a lawmaker from the junior governing coalition partner SPD.
An "undignified spectacle," were the words used by the Handelsblatt daily business publication to describe it.
Fire flares up again overnight at Hitler's mountain retreat
A fire that broke out on Friday evening at the Eagle's Nest mountain retreat in southern Germany that was once used by Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler erupted again overnight to Sunday in the almost destroyed building, Bavarian police said.
A police officer said flames there burnt again at "room height" after smoldering embers provoked a flare-up in what the officer said was a common occurrence in the case of such conflagrations.
The renewed fire triggered another deployment of firefighters to the site, known as Kehlsteinhaus in German, at the top of the Obersalzberg mountain.
The site, formerly used by Hitler to receive diplomats and other foreign guests, has been a restaurant since 1952 but was closed on Friday when the fire broke out. No one was injured.
Police arrested a 33-year-old German man suspected of having lit the fire, with an initial psychiatric assessement indicating mental illness.
The building was largely destroyed by the blaze, which caused millions of euros of damage.
IN DEPTH: Audi defends decision to open plant in US
After US President Donald Trump on Saturday announced that car producer Audi would build a $4 billion (€3.77 billion) assembly plant in the state of Georgia, the company has defended its planned move against criticism that it goes against German interests.
"This decision was preceded by many months of careful planning and intense negotiations," CEO Gerbot Döllner told reporters on Sunday.
"If the American president invites you, you accept the invitation. That is what respect for the office and for the country in which we invest demands," he said, arguing that the plan could protect jobs in Germany by boosting the carmaker's global business.
The move is yet to be approved by the supervisory board of Volkswagen, which owns Audi.
You can read more here: Trump announces Audi will build $4 billion factory in US.
German Environmental Prize goes to climate-action lawyer and wastewater engineer
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has presented this year's prestigious German Environmental Prize, worth €500,000 ($560,150), to a lawyer specializing in environmental cases and an engineer who has developed high-performance filters for wastewater plants.
At a ceremony in the western city of Aachen, Steinmeier commended Hamburg-based lawyer Roda Verheyen and engineer Klaus Vossenkaul as models of environmental protection.
"They show that each and every individual can make a difference," he said.
According to the German Federal Environmental Foundation (DBU), which awards the prize, Verheyen received the honor for "getting justice done for the environment."
In his speech, Steinmeier said she had shown many people ways to fight for their interests amid human-induced climate change.
Among other things, he said, her constitutional complaint against the climate protection law in 2021 played a decisive role in the Constitutional Court's ruling that Germany should become climate-neutral by 2045.
Speaking about Vossenkaul, Steinmeier said the engineer was a prime example of "creativity and inventiveness" in the field of environmental protection.
The president said the membrane technology developed by Vossenkaul helped to make wastewater plants more economical in terms of space, energy and cost, thus protecting "our basis of life."
Most expect coalition government to fall before end of term — survey
Just one in four people in Germany (23%) believes that the coalition of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative bloc and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) will last its full term till the next federal elections at the start of 2029, a survey has shown.
Some 44% said they believed the coalition would end within the next two years, according to the YouGov survey of 2,202 eligible voters, while around 13% are even convinced that the coalition will not see out the year.
Conservative voters who support parties in the so-called Union — the alliance of Christian Democrats (CDU) and Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) — are less optimistic about the coalition's continued existence than SPD supporters.
A whole 53% of CDU/CSU voters expect a premature end to the coalition, compared with just 32% who think it will last out its term.
That compares with the 46% of SPD voters who doubt the coalition's long-term viability, with 34% trusting it will cohere until 2029.
Twenty percent gave no opinion on the issue.
The coalition has been divided over a reform of Germany's pension and welfare systems, as well as over the best way to deal with the challenge posed by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which beat the mainstream parties in recent state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Football: Bayern Munich coach Kompany to remain in hospital after collapse
Bayern Munich head coach Vincent Kompany is set to remain in hospital for several days and will be missing for a number of weeks after collapsing at the club's training center on Friday.
The 40-year-old Belgian had recently been suffering from a virus and collapsed while observing a reserve team training session.
"The good news is he's stable," said Bayern's director of sport, Max Eberl, on Saturday. "I spoke with him last night, and with his wife too. It wasn't a nice moment for any of us. He collapsed on the pitch yesterday and will spend a few more days in hospital until everything is checked over."
Eberl said that doctors are "trying to find out what it is," adding: "The tests have already yielded some results, but further results are needed to determine exactly what it is and how long it will take for him to recover."
Eberl said it will be a while before Kompany is fit to return to work. "We're not talking in terms of days, but weeks," he said. "We're all clear on that."
Kompany will miss Bayern's game away at high-flying SC Freiburg on Sunday, with assistant coach Aaron Danks set to stand in for him. He will also miss next week's Bundesliga Klassiker at home to Borussia Dortmund and the difficult trip to Atletico Madrid in the Champions League on November 3.
"It shows again that health is the most important thing in life, not football," said Eberl, stressing that Kompany will "only come back when he's fit."
Bayern will also travel to Freiburg on Sunday without captain Joshua Kimmich, whose father passed away aged 57 this week.
Goalkeeper Manuel Neuer will also miss the game due to "persistent tendonitis" in his foot, as will defender Min-jae Kim, playmaker Jamal Musiala and forward Luiz Diaz.
Ryanair closes base, cuts routes at Berlin's international airport
Low-cost Irish airline Ryanair has closed its base at Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER), and removed 12 routes there at the start of its winter timetable.
The move was announced in April and confirmed in October, with the airline having long complained about high taxes and fees at German airports.
Six of the 12 deleted routes, from BER to Palermo, Marseille, Triest, Reggio Calabria, Tallin and Pisa, can now no longer be directly reached on flights from the airport, the airline and the airport operator FBB said.
The other six — Gran Canaria, Fuerteventura, Lanzarote, Bologna, Thessaloniki and Vilnius — are served by other airlines flying from BER.
The seven Ryanair aircraft that were based at the BER airport have been reassigned to airports in European Union countries that, according to Ryanair, have got rid of aviation taxes or reduced airport charges.
Ryanair is to still fly to and from Berlin using planes based elsewhere.
The operators of BER have pointed out that despite Ryanair's move, eight more destinations can be reached from the airport than last winter, as other airlines have expanded their services at the airport.
  
Welcome back as we resume our Germany coverage
Guten Morgen from DW's newsroom in Bonn as we return to our reporting on the German stories currently hitting the headlines.
We will be looking again at developments as a fire at the Eagle's Nest mountain retreat in southern Germany once used by Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler flared up again overnight.
Meanwhile, a survey has shown that most people in Germany do not believe the current conservative/center-left coalition under Chancellor Friedrich Merz will last the full four-year course of its term.
And Europe's largest low-cost carrier, Ryanair, is closing its base at Berlin's international airport as previously announced, meaing that 50% of the carrier's flights there will be cut.
Read on here for more on stories from and about Germany.
We're pausing coverage today
We're pausing our coverage of the weekend's news out of Germany until later on Sunday morning.
Hope to see you then! Bis morgen früh!
WATCH: Hitler's mountaintop 'Eagle's Nest' goes up in flames
An overnight fire engulfed Eagle's Nest, a historic Nazi-era site once used by Adolf Hitler in Germany's Bavarian Alps. Firefighters faced difficult conditions battling the flames at the mountaintop location, while one suspect has been taken into temporary custody. Police are looking into whether this is a potential case of arson.
DW spoke to historian Sven Keller of the Obersalzberg Documentation Center about the site's historical significance, why it was preserved, and how Germany deals with landmarks associated with its Nazi past.
German national facing trial over alleged attempt to join 'Islamic Sate'
Germany's prosecutor's office said that a German national has been placed in pre-trial detention for allegedly attempting to join the so-called "Islamic State" terror group, while abroad, German news agency dpa reported.
The agency cited a spokeswoman for the Federal Prosecutor's Office as saying that an arrest warrant had been executed and that a 21-year-old was extradited to Germany.
The suspect is accused of travelling to Ethiopia from Berlin in January 2025, with the purpose of joining the IS terror group in Somalia and receive training there.
Prosecutors allege that he never reached Somalia, but instead traveled to Pakistan to join Islamic State, where he was reportedly arrrested in February 2025.
The suspect stands accused of attempted membership in a terrorist organization abroad. He is also accused of preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state.
Merz highlights threat from Russia
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz highlighted the threat Germany faces from extremist parties to foreign enemies, including a "massive threat" from Russia.
"How do we safeguard our freedom and our security in Europe, in the face of growing threats from extremists within and foreign powers from without?" the chancellor said, adding that Russia was seeking "to destabilise Germany on a daily basis."
Germany is one of the biggest military and political supporters of Ukraine and has been on high alert for acts of sabotage in recent months.
That's especially since an explosive-laden drone was discovered near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport. Berlin said Moscow was behind the attempted attack.
In one of the most recent incidents, on Thursday, police in the German state of Brandenburg arrested a Ukrainian man on suspicion of spying for Russia.
No change to 'firewall' when it comes to AfD, says Merz
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz once again stood firm on any notion of ever working with Germany's far-right.
Merx restated his opposition to any change in the"firewall" policy of isolating the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) at the CSU conference in Munich.
"Anyone who feels they have to vote for these people has no place in our Union. They have no place amongst us," Merz said.
The AfD, has been topping national opinion polls although a Friday poll showed Merz's conservative bloc closing the gap.
Nevertheless, according to the poll, Merz's coalition would still fall short of a majority were an election to be held.
The poll, conducted for public broadcaster ZDF, asked voters which party they would support if a federal election were held this Sunday.

title: »Tatort«-Vote: Wie gefiel Ihnen »Gottesgarten« mit Rosalie Thomass?
content_c:
Krimi-Vote Wie gefiel Ihnen der Franken-»Tatort« mit Rosalie Thomass?
Ein Mord in einem Nürnberger Stundenhotel führte zu einem alten Missbrauchsfall in der oberfränkischen Provinz. Das Opfer, ein queerer Sexarbeiter, war in seiner Jugend auf einer Party von einem Erwachsenen unter Drogen gesetzt und vergewaltigt worden.
Kommissar Voss (Fabian Hinrichs) und seine neue Kollegin Emilia Rathgeber (Rosalie Thomass) stießen bei ihren Ermittlungen auf zwei Jugendfreunde, die Zeugen des Missbrauchs gewesen waren und nun den Täter zur Rechenschaft ziehen wollten. Endlos wurden in diesem »Tatort« in Rückblenden die gewaltsamen Partyszenen gezeigt; der damals gespielte Partyhit »Ohne dich (schlaf’ ich heut Nacht nicht ein)« von Münchner Freiheit hallte dabei von der Filmvergangenheit in die Filmgegenwart nach.
Dramatischer Höhepunkt: Einer der Freunde des Opfers erschießt den Peiniger von einst – und die dazu gestürmte neue Kommissarin erschießt den Opferfreund.
Ein bisschen angepappt wirkte die Szene, in der erklärt wurde, dass der getötete Fiesling nicht nur diese eine Vergewaltigung begangen hatte, sondern im Darknet auch noch einen Handelsplatz für kinderpornografische Darstellungen betrieb. Das wirkte, als wollten die Verantwortlichen ein wenig das Blutbad am Ende legitimieren.
- 
2 Min
In unserer Kritik schrieben wir: »Harter Fall, zarter Neuanfang. Knapp zehn Jahre lang ermittelte Voss an der Seite der von Dagmar Manzel verkörperten Kommissarin Ringelhahn, mit der ihn eine Art platonische Liebe verband. Die Annäherungsszenen an die neue Kollegin gehören zu den schönsten Momenten im Krimi, weil Vieles angedeutet bleibt und sich doch langsam eine Vertrautheit einspielt. Regisseur Dustin Loose hat zuvor unter anderem die bewegende, makellose Folge um eine trans Zeugin gedreht. Auch im neuen Franken-›Tatort‹ gibt es intensive leise Momente. Die Provinz- und Partyszenen wirken indes überwiegend überreizt und ausgewalzt.«
Wir gaben 6 von 10 Punkten. Was halten Sie von dem Krimi?
Einen zweiten gemeinsamen Fall haben Fabian Hinrichs und Rosalie Thomass bereits abgedreht. Er trägt den Titel »Totholz« und handelt vom Tod an einer 13-Jährigen. Regie führte Kilian Riedhof, der in der Vergangenheit für spektakuläre Fernsehprojekte wie den Zweiteiler »Gladbeck« stand und zuletzt unter anderem in Frankreich das Kinodrama »Meinen Hass bekommt ihr nicht« über den Terroranschlag auf der Pariser Konzerthaus Bataclan 2015 gedreht hatte.
description: In Nürnberg trat Rosalie Thomass als Kommissarin Emilia Rathgeber ihren »Tatort«-Dienst an – und geriet am Ende in ein überreiztes Blutbad. Oder sind Sie anderer Meinung?

title: Kreuzfahrtschiff rammt zwei Containerschiffe in Bremerhaven
content_c:
Bremerhaven Kreuzfahrtschiff rammt zwei Containerschiffe
Das Kreuzfahrtschiff "Mein Schiff 3" ist nach dem Auslaufen in Bremerhaven bei stürmischem Wetter mit zwei Schiffen kollidiert. Zwei Schlepper wurden beschädigt. Nach aktuellem Stand gab es keine Verletzten.
Der Unfall geschah bei stürmischem Wetter beim Ablegen von der Columbuskaje. Auf einem von der Deutschen Presse-Agentur verifizierten Augenzeugenvideo ist zu sehen, wie das Kreuzfahrtschiff von Schleppern begleitet bei deutlichem Wellengang ausläuft.
Der Abstand zu einem an der Hafenmauer liegenden Containerschiff wird immer kleiner, dann rammt das Kreuzfahrtschiff das Containerschiff, das Video ruckelt. "Ich glaube, das war es mit der Reise", sagt eine Frau in dem Video. Auf den Bildern sind Trümmer zu sehen. Die "Mein Schiff 3" und Rettungsboote wurden demnach beschädigt.
Mehr als 3.000 Menschen an Bord
Die "Mein Schiff 3" liegt inzwischen wieder an der Columbuskaje (Archivbild).
Tui Cruises bestätigte den Unfall. Eine Sprecherin sagte allerdings, das Schiff sei nur mit einem Containerschiff zusammengestoßen und nicht mit zwei. Die "Mein Schiff 3" sei wieder am Pier, wo der entstandene Schaden begutachtet werde. Zum Unfallzeitpunkt waren demnach 2.428 Gäste und 922 Crewmitglieder an Bord. Verletzte gebe es nicht. Alle könnten vorerst an Bord bleiben, so die Sprecherin. Fachleute seien vor Ort und untersuchten die Lage. "Weitere Informationen werden wir bereitstellen, sobald gesicherte Erkenntnisse vorliegen."
Am frühen Sonntagabend war zunächst von einer Kollision zwischen dem Kreuzfahrtschiff "Mein Schiff 3" und einem Containerschiff die Rede. Später teilte die Polizei mit, dass insgesamt drei Schiffe betroffen sind. Laut dem Bremer Häfenressort gab es keinen Wassereinbruch bei den betroffenen Schiffen. In einem der Containerschiffe entstand demnach jedoch ein zehn Meter langer Riss.

title: Магнітна буря 26 жовтня: кому буде найгірше і як себе вберегти
content_c:
Магнітна буря 26 жовтня: кому буде найгірше і як себе вберегти
За попередніми розрахунками, протягом дня суттєвого посилення геомагнітних коливань не передбачається.
У понеділок, 26 жовтня, сильна магнітна буря не очікується.
За даними триденного прогнозу NOAA, планетарний індекс Kp протягом доби переважно становитиме 2, а наприкінці дня може піднятися приблизно до 2,33.
Водночас прогноз може оновлюватися, адже активність Сонця змінюється. Тому для точного розуміння ситуації варто стежити за свіжими даними космічної погоди, особливо якщо показники почнуть помітно зростати.
Чому виникають магнітні бурі на Землі
Магнітні бурі пов’язані з процесами, які відбуваються на Сонці. Сонячні спалахи та викиди корональної маси можуть супроводжуватися вивільненням значної кількості енергії.
Під час цих явищ у космічний простір потрапляють потоки заряджених частинок, серед яких протони та електрони.
Коли збурення сонячного вітру досягають магнітосфери Землі, вони можуть спричиняти коливання її магнітного поля. Інтенсивність цих коливань залежить від характеристик сонячного вітру та взаємодії міжпланетного магнітного поля із земною магнітосферою.
Як зменшити вплив магнітних бур
- Нормалізувати сон. Спати не менше восьми годин на добу
- Збалансувати водний баланс. Пити протягом дня чисту воду
- Передивитися щоденний раціон. Надати перевагу легким стравам і відмовитися від алкоголю

title: В Португалии полиция разогнала протесты жильцов и демонтировала палаточные лагеря
content_c:
В Португалии 25 октября полиция разогнала палаточные лагеря участников протестов против роста цен на жилье в Лиссабоне и Порту, применив дубинки и задействовав служебных собак. Операции провели ночью после нескольких дней столкновений на акциях против подорожания жилья. Об этом сообщило издание The Guardian.
Десятки полицейских, часть из которых со служебными собаками, начали операцию на площади Росиу в центре Лиссабона вскоре после двух часов ночи. Там демонтировали более 100 палаток. Правоохранители также разобрали меньший лагерь на площади Дона Жуана I в Порту, где стояло около 50 палаток. Во время разгона против участников применили дубинки. Депутат от партии «Левый блок» Фабиан Фигейреду назвал действия полиции ударом по демократии Португалии.
«Борьба за жилье — это право. Как и мирный протест. Конституция гарантирует и то, и другое. Давайте продолжим — ради нашего будущего», — отметил политик.
Лиссабонский лагерь возник после многотысячного шествия по одной из главных улиц столицы. Люди протестовали против цен на жилье, которые стали недоступными для граждан со средними доходами. Участники португальских акций вдохновлялись подобными лагерями в Испании. Они устанавливали палатки на центральных площадях, требуя ответа на усугубляющийся жилищный кризис.
Полиция назвала свои действия соразмерными и заявила, что сначала призывала участников добровольно покинуть лагеря. По её сообщению, в двух городах задержали 31 человека за неповиновение и убрали 171 конструкцию. Правоохранители также сообщили об 11 пострадавших, среди которых трое полицейских.
Из задержанных в Лиссабоне 25 человек были освобождены с обязательством явиться в суд в понедельник, 26 октября. Организация Casa Para Viver, название которой означает «Дом для жизни», оспорила официальные данные о пострадавших. Она обвинила власти в силовом подавлении протеста и призвала к новым акциям в среду, 28 октября.
«Выбрать раннее утро, чтобы задействовать полицейских собак и стрелять резиновыми пулями в людей, которые спали или мирно протестовали, — это политическое решение. Это показывает, что данное правительство предпочитает подавлять тех, кто выступает против жилищного кризиса, вместо того чтобы решить сам кризис», — заявили в Casa Para Viver.
Палаточное противостояние в Португалии началось в начале октября. Активисты разбили лагерь в Порту, после чего полиция его разогнала. Вскоре подобные акции начались в Лиссабоне. Повторные столкновения между правоохранителями и участниками сопровождались десятками задержаний и сообщениями о пострадавших.
Волна недовольства охватила различные европейские города. В Испании и Португалии одной из главных причин протестов стала стоимость жилья, которая лишила многих местных жителей возможности приобрести или арендовать жилье. В Португалии цены на недвижимость с 2017 года выросли более чем вдвое. Аренда за это время подорожала почти вдвое. Страна столкнулась с одним из самых острых в Европе кризисов доступности жилья.
Местные жители давно жалуются на последствия стремительного роста рынка недвижимости. Они связывают его с либерализацией правил, выдачей так называемых золотых виз, программами для цифровых кочевников и распространением краткосрочной аренды. По их мнению, эти изменения усилили финансовое давление на тех, кто постоянно проживает в стране.
Протестующие требуют от правоцентристского правительства отказаться от предложенных законодательных изменений. Они предусматривают упрощение выселений и отмену ограничений на размер арендной платы по новым договорам. Законопроект уже прошел первое чтение в парламенте. Активисты выступают против его дальнейшего принятия.
Напомним, что 24 октября протесты из-за роста стоимости жизни прошли и в крупных городах Италии. В Турине, Риме и Болонье демонстранты вступили в столкновения с полицией. Власти усилили меры безопасности, а многие магазины заранее закрылись из-за риска повреждений. Полиция также задержала человека, подозреваемого в причастности к организации протестного «Движения 17 октября».
Кроме того, во Франции 24 октября массовые демонстрации сопровождались столкновениями, а МВД сообщило о почти тысяче задержаний. По оценкам правительства, на улицы по всей стране вышли не менее 400 тысяч человек. Участники поддерживали требования старшеклассников увеличить количество учителей и отремонтировать учебные корпуса. Люди также протестовали против высокой стоимости жизни и силовой реакции властей на общественное недовольство.

title: ЗСУ зірвали плани РФ щодо оточення на Донбасі та звільнили майже 280 кв. км під Лиманом – ISW
content_c:
Сили оборони України рішуче розгромили основний російський наступ, спрямований на повне захоплення Донецької області у 2026 році, та утримували ініціативу в ключових секторах лінії фронту протягом більшої частини року, повідомляє Інститут вивчення війни (ISW).
За оцінкою аналітиків, українські підрозділи завдали операційної поразки північному угрупованню військ РФ на Лиманському напрямку, тим самим зірвавши задум російського командування провести широке оточення українського укріпленого району.
"Операція "Вівальді" призвела до звільнення близько 277 квадратних кілометрів території та 16 населених пунктів на північ і північний схід від Лимана", – зазначається у звіті ISW з посиланням на оприлюднені дані командування 3-го армійського корпусу ЗСУ під керівництвом бригадного генерала Андрія Білецького.
В інституті констатують, що операція складалася з чотирьох фаз, перші підсумки яких українське командування почало оголошувати у вересні 2026 року, хоча фактичні наступальні дії розпочалися орієнтовно в березні поточного року.
Джерело: https://x.com/TheStudyofWar/status/2114439340092760233?s=20

title: Musk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection as service restored
content_c:
Musk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection as service restored
- Published
Elon Musk has said his company SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink internet service, after Ukrainian officials said connectivity issues appeared to have been resolved.
The tech billionaire accused Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using it for military activity - but denied being responsible for a simultaneous issue with its US-run, military-grade counterpart Starshield.
Kyiv has not officially commented on Musk's latest claim but Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said his post was "very strange".
Musk had earlier denied deliberately throttling Ukraine's connection, which it says hampered its ability to conduct defensive operations for more than a week.
The issue first emerged last week during a broader row between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
Musk's latest comments, and the seeming restoration of the service, came after US President Donald Trump said he had told the Tesla and X owner to "put it back", having repeatedly denied instructing him to limit the service.
"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X on Saturday.
"Ukraine['s] military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."
He went on to say that SpaceX had "done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth" and reiterated his stipulation that Starshield was a different system and controlled by the US government, adding: "What they decide to do is up to them."
He added in a later post: "[Starlink] can be used for infrastructure that is military, but it cannot be used for unequivocally offensive strikes that make it fair game to be struck back."
Reacting to Musk's post, Beskrestnov said that drones operating via Starlink in Ukraine had a speed restriction of 70-90km/h (43-56mph) and did not work on Russian territory.
"Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and medium-range strikes," he wrote on Telegram.
"It is very strange that Elon Musk is not aware of Starlink restrictions in Ukraine."
There was no immediate comment from Ukraine's defence ministry.
Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed, both of which run on networks of low Earth orbit satellites launched by SpaceX.
Starlink allows military units to co-ordinate, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield, while Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones.
Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.
Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said earlier on Saturday that the military was now recording a "stable connection", with drones now able to reach speeds in excess of 400km/h. Kyiv previously said the connection would cut out above 161km/h.
"The speeds are now where they need to be," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
Musk did not disclose in his post why SpaceX had chosen to make the change to its service last week, when Ukraine's extensive use of Starlink had been known for several years.
The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic standoff between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.
While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war.
Faced with midterm elections next month and domestic displeasure with rising fuel prices, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal with Moscow - criticised by European allies as funding Russia's war machine - to supply Russian diesel to the US and the global market.
Zelensky initially agreed to cease strikes targeting Russian oil facilities on the proviso that Moscow cease striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, before restarting the strikes after several instances of Russia disregarding this.
The Ukrainian leader said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.
- Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap? 
  - Published1 day ago
Fighting and aerial attacks continued to be exchanged between Russia and Ukraine overnight.
Ukraine's emergency services said three people were killed and 15 others injured, including an 11-year-old girl, in attacks on the Dnipropetrovsk region, in the south east.
Another six people were injured when a Russian drone struck an apartment block in the central city of Vinnytsia, it said.
The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday that it had struck a cargo vessel it claimed was being used to supply the Ukrainian army while it was en route to the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk overnight.
It also said Russian forces hit a logistics centre, a distribution centre and a logistics terminal in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv.
Ukraine's defence ministry earlier said it struck a facility in the Russian city of Oryol run by a sanctioned heavy machinery manufacturer. Russian authorities said three people were killed in the strike.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, with fighting now into its fifth year.

"The speeds are now where they need to be," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
Musk did not disclose in his post why SpaceX had chosen to make the change to its service last week, when Ukraine's extensive use of Starlink had been known for several years.
The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic standoff between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.
While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war.
Faced with midterm elections next month and domestic displeasure with rising fuel prices, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal with Moscow - criticised by European allies as funding Russia's war machine - to supply Russian diesel to the US and the global market.
Zelensky initially agreed to cease strikes targeting Russian oil facilities on the proviso that Moscow cease striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, before restarting the strikes after several instances of Russia disregarding this.
The Ukrainian leader said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.
- Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap? 
  - Published1 day ago
Fighting and aerial attacks continued to be exchanged between Russia and Ukraine overnight.
Ukraine's emergency services said three people were killed and 15 others injured, including an 11-year-old girl, in attacks on the Dnipropetrovsk region, in the south east.
Another six people were injured when a Russian drone struck an apartment block in the central city of Vinnytsia, it said.
The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday that it had struck a cargo vessel it claimed was being used to supply the Ukrainian army while it was en route to the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk overnight.
It also said Russian forces hit a logistics centre, a distribution centre and a logistics terminal in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv.
Ukraine's defence ministry earlier said it struck a facility in the Russian city of Oryol run by a sanctioned heavy machinery manufacturer. Russian authorities said three people were killed in the strike.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, with fighting now into its fifth year.

title: Signs suggest Thomas Markle Sr may be ‘sex offender of the grossest kind’, says Philippine minister
content_c:
All signs point to Thomas Markle Sr being a “possible sex offender of the grossest kind” although a full forensic investigation will give a “definitive picture”, the Philippine interior minister has told the Guardian.
Authorities in the south-east Asian country are analysing digital images allegedly belonging to the estranged father of the Duchess of Sussex that were said to have been found at his former home in Cebu. Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, reported to authorities last week that he had apparently discovered a stash of child sexual abuse images.
The duchess, already estranged from her father, broke off all contact with him last year, reportedly telling him she and the authorities were aware of allegations he had abused young girls, it is understood.
In a final letter to her father first reported by the Sun on Sunday, sent while he was in a hospital in the Philippines having had a leg amputated, Meghan made clear he would never see his grandchildren Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, and that she would never contact him again, it is understood.
Jonvic Remulla, the Philippine interior minister, told the Guardian: “In these cases where family disputes are mixed up, we have to consider all the angles. Right now all signs point to a possible sex offender of the grossest kind. We want to be sure before we release the findings. The forensics data will be complete in a week.”
Remulla said a statement would be released once the data had been analysed, without giving a specific date. “Please give us a week to determine the contents and to come up with a definitive picture,” he said. “We will release a statement then.”
Markle Sr has denied possessing child sexual abuse images, telling the Daily Mail the accusations were “sick lies”. Philippine police are also investigating a laptop found at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr had been living until he returned to the US earlier this year.
In a statement given to Agence France-Presse, Remulla said the Philippine national police inspected Markle’s former home and found a “trove of child pornography materials as well as a laptop”.
“The PNP will coordinate with their counterparts to locate and take appropriate legal actions against Mr Markle if found that there is sufficient evidence to charge him,” he said.
Markle Sr has told the Mail the computers had not been in his possession since he left Mexico with his son in 2025 and moved to the Philippines “for a fresh start”. He said: “This is bullshit. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.”
The Sun reported on Friday that Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu. Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the newspaper said.
Meghan has revealed she learned of allegations against her father in 2019, having been told by the Metropolitan police, and said she was given assurances these claims were being investigated. Sources said she had been advised that speaking publicly about the claims could have jeopardised any potential legal case and also put her at risk of legal action.
On Saturday the Met confirmed it had passed a letter “containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom” to Meghan and the Duke of Sussex in 2019 but did not share details with other law enforcement agencies. Scotland Yard is considering whether to refer itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct to review its actions.
The duchess was “upset and really frustrated” that the Met had not acted on allegations made in that letter, sources said.
In a new interview with the Mail on Sunday, Markle Sr said he had “never had sex with anyone under the age of 18”, telling the paper that when he was single he travelled to the Philippines at least twice and paid for sex.
He is reportedly in a Florida rehabilitation centre after his leg amputation.
In a statement on Friday, Meghan said she was “deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed”.
She said: “In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.
“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.
“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”
Sources later clarified she had misremembered the year in which the Met had contacted her, and confirmed it had been 2019, not 2018 as she said on Friday.
The FBI said in a statement on Friday that it was “aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of US law.”
