title: France: Hundreds arrested after nationwide protests
content_c:
France: Hundreds arrested after nationwide protests
Published October 24, 2026last updated October 25, 2026
What you need to know
- More than 1,000 people were arrested after protesters took to the streets on Saturday
- The French government said 410,000 people took part in protests across the country, though unions put the tally higher
- Clashes broke out between protesters and police in cities like Paris, Marseille and Lyon, with police having deploying tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds
- French police deployed more than 70,000 police and elite security forces across France to contain the unrest
This blog is now closed. Thank you for reading.
You can read all our updates on the protests and unrest in France and other parts of Europe on October 24 and 25, 2026, below.
Le Pen launches campaign with impassioned speech
Marine Le Pen launched her fourth bid to become president of France on Sunday with a plea to "French patriots" to back her and her far-right National Rally (RN) in spring elections.
The grande dame of the far-right, Le Pen delivered an impassioned invocation of French spirit in Orleans, calling for "a renaissance" of the country's virtues and stressing its rich creative and intellectual history.
She blasted "Little Marquis Macron" and the state of France under his stewardship — both domestically and internationally — offering a fiery outline of the need to restore order, but also civility in the country, alongside promises of maintaining French (nuclear) defense and judicial sovereignty.
Le Pen said "we'll protect our public spaces so that they can remain places full of life and mutual respect" and cited civility as the surest way to keep violence out of society.
She praised regionalism over globalism or supranationalism in the form of the European Union (EU), and spoke of the need to defend freedom and the "French way of life," making clear that, "In France, you live like the French."
Le Pen recalled General Charles de Gaulle several times throughout her speech, emphasizing the historic importance of the moment when it comes to securing the promise of the future.
After ending her remarks with a full-throated "Vive la France!," a relieved-looking Le Pen was joined on stage by heir apparent Jordan Bardella and party members for a rousing rendition of the national anthem under the campaign slogan, "Pour la France La Renaissance."
WATCH: France protests continue despite police crackdown
Amid the latest demonstrations, what's driving the unrest, and could a broader youth-led protest movement be taking shape?
French unions and protest groups call for more rallies
French unions and protest groups have called for fresh demonstrations on October 31 and a nationwide strike on November 5 to maintain pressure on the government.
The left-wing Solidaires union federation said anger over wages, living costs and public services was bringing together students, workers, firefighters and other groups.
"We see an aggregation of anger," Solidaires co-leader Murielle Guilbert told broadcaster BFM TV.
The SUD Education teaching union said it would join the October 31 demonstrations. The larger CGT union is set to decide during the week.
The Yellow Vests movement also called for rallies, including sit-ins outside town halls and the National Assembly.
The government has opened talks with unions and student representatives, but protest leaders say its proposals are inadequate.
France reports more than 1,300 arrests after protests
French authorities detained 1,314 people during nationwide protests on Saturday, according to a provisional Interior Ministry tally.
The ministry said 53 police officers and other security personnel were injured, firefighters responded to 75 fires and 24 businesses were looted. It did not provide a figure for injured protesters.
Clashes broke out in cities including Paris, Marseille, Bordeaux, Toulouse and Tours, with police using tear gas. The ministry blamed groups including radical far-left activists for confrontations along or near protest routes.
Authorities counted 410,000 participants at 289 demonstrations and gatherings, down from 550,000 a week earlier. Other estimates put Saturday's turnout as high as 800,000.
The reported arrests and violence were substantially lower than on October 17, when authorities recorded 2,628 detentions and 1,144 injured security personnel.
The ministry said several investigations had been opened and described the subsequent night as calm.
Authorities say nearly 1,000 arrested after day of protests in France
With Saturday's protest over, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez reported nearly 1,000 arrests.
The number is expected to rise as security officials tally up the day's events, Nunez added.
"Multiple lootings have been averted," he said.
While some clashes between protesters and police were reported in many French cities, the scope of the unrest was much smaller compared to the protests last Saturday, which saw buildings defaced and burned, and some 1,500 shops looted across the country.
Nunez previously put the number of people arrested last weekend at 2,700.
WATCH: Could the unrest play into the hands of Le Pen's National Rally party?
Here's what to know if you are joining us now
Some 410,000 people marched across France on Saturday, according to the country's interior ministry, as the country braced for a possible repeat of violence seen last weekend.
In Paris alone, at least 110,000 people turned out to denounce rising living costs and growing inequality.
Police were out in force in major French cities. While rallies in Paris and Marseille were mostly peaceful, clashes between protesters and police were reported in towards the evening.
Riot police in Paris fired tear gas and water cannons at some 500 hooded youths before they eventually dispersed. In Marseille, youths blocked roads by setting trash cans on fire. They threw rocks and bottles at security forces.
Clashes were also reported in the cities of Lyon, Bordeaux, Grenoble, Clermont-Ferrand, Lille, Rennes, Nantes and Toulouse.
Altercations during protests are not sight unseen in France, DW reporter on the ground says
France is known for its protest culture, where demonstration is considered a bedrock value.
Altercations between the police and demonstrators are by and large part of the French protest ritual.
What we are seeing could even be considered a relatively calm end-of-demonstration situation, Lisa Louis, who is in Paris, said.
Milan: Protests less unruly than last weekend amid high security
Meanwhile, security guards were deployed in Milan on Saturday amid demonstrations against the rising cost of living.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni ordered 500 soldiers to be dispatched to the city, in addition to about 5,000 police and other law enforcement personnel there.
But the protests in the large Italian city were less unruly than last weekend, when looters ransacked businesses near the central Duomo area. Around 3,000 people rallied in Milan, with another smaller demonstration taking place in Rome.
IN PICTURES: Clashes break out between police and protesters in demonstrations across France
As the day went on (and largely toward the end of demonstrations in many cities), clashes occurred between protesters and the authorities during the demonstrations across France. 
At least 400,000 people have taken part in protests across France
The French interior ministry said it estimates 410,000 people to have taken part in protest throughout France today.
Demonstrations were set to take place in Paris and Marseille but protesters took to the streets in other cities for rallies like Lyon and Nantes.
There were reports about clashes between protesters and police in several cities, including Paris.
There were protests in the city of Lyon, in the east-central part of France, where police used tear gas to disperse protesters wearing masks.
There are also reports about clashes in Marseille, where police fired tear gas to disperse crowds.
About 550,000 people attended demonstrations throughout the country last weekend.
French protests nowhere near the looting seen last weekend as yet, says DW reporter on the ground
The mood over the past few days in France felt almost a bit apocalyptic. Business owners told me they were worried more looting might lie ahead, after gangs of individuals had ransacked and destroyed at least 3,000 shops across the country last weekend.
"Some of us are planning to buy weapons to defend ourselves, in case the pillagers come back. One day, there's going to be a tragedy — for sure," Jonathan Siad, owner of a tobacco shop in Paris, said to me.
Other store owners were too afraid to talk to us in front of the camera – they worried criminals might see the interview and target their shop.
Residents told me they would try to avoid the area where the demonstration was taking place. Only to add that they hoped the situation wouldn't escalate like last week, when even places far away from the actual marches became hotspots of clashes between the police and protesters.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez had admitted on Monday a "loss of control" last Saturday. The authorities thus increased the number of police deployed across France by 10,000 to 70,000 this Saturday.
First clashes between protesters and the police started to occur in the late afternoon in several cities across France such as Marseille, Lyon and Paris.
But for now, the much feared mass looting and ransacking doesn't seem to be happening. The situation is nowhere near the total chaos Paris and other cities like Marseille experienced last Saturday.
"Last weekend, our neighborhood resembled a war zone with gangs roaming the area. Today, it's completely empty apart from police with their vans," Yassaman Metghalchi, co-owner of a jewelry shop in the city center of Paris that got looted last Saturday, told me.
"All of our neighbors feel reassured – although the night is still young and we need to wait and see what will happen," she added.
Paris police say 110,000 protesters on Saturday in 'City of Lights'
Paris police say 110,000 protesters were on the streets in the city on Saturday. The anti-government "Yellow Vest" movementteamed up with aggrieved school students for this round of demonstrations.
The CGT trade union, meanwhile, said 800,000 participated in protests across France, with 250,000 people taking part in Paris.
Saturday's protesters were limited by Parisian authorities to the city's southeastern edge, away from the center.
Authorities prepared to help the protesters march safely from the Place d'Italie in the 13th arrondissement on the left bank of the Seine River to Porte de Vincennes which lies further away on the right bank.
A post on X by Paris Police Prefecture showed the Porte d'Italie from the sky ahead of the march.
French news agency AFP reported clashes in Paris after the demonstrations.
French use tear gas at protests in Lyon, Lille, Toulouse and Nantes
The French police used tear gas in response to protests in the southeastern city of Lyon. Use of tear gas was also reported in the cities of Lille, Toulouse and Nantes.
Protests against Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally in Orleans
In Orleans, south of Paris, protesters also came out to the streets against a two-day congress held in the city of Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party.
According to polls, Le Pen is the frontrunner in France's presidential elections next year.
description: The French government says more than 1,000 people were arrested following nationwide protests on Saturday. Police and elite security forces were out in force across the country as clashes broke out.

"Some of us are planning to buy weapons to defend ourselves, in case the pillagers come back. One day, there's going to be a tragedy — for sure," Jonathan Siad, owner of a tobacco shop in Paris, said to me.
Other store owners were too afraid to talk to us in front of the camera – they worried criminals might see the interview and target their shop.
Residents told me they would try to avoid the area where the demonstration was taking place. Only to add that they hoped the situation wouldn't escalate like last week, when even places far away from the actual marches became hotspots of clashes between the police and protesters.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez had admitted on Monday a "loss of control" last Saturday. The authorities thus increased the number of police deployed across France by 10,000 to 70,000 this Saturday.
First clashes between protesters and the police started to occur in the late afternoon in several cities across France such as Marseille, Lyon and Paris.
But for now, the much feared mass looting and ransacking doesn't seem to be happening. The situation is nowhere near the total chaos Paris and other cities like Marseille experienced last Saturday.
"Last weekend, our neighborhood resembled a war zone with gangs roaming the area. Today, it's completely empty apart from police with their vans," Yassaman Metghalchi, co-owner of a jewelry shop in the city center of Paris that got looted last Saturday, told me.
"All of our neighbors feel reassured – although the night is still young and we need to wait and see what will happen," she added.
Paris police say 110,000 protesters on Saturday in 'City of Lights'
Paris police say 110,000 protesters were on the streets in the city on Saturday. The anti-government "Yellow Vest" movementteamed up with aggrieved school students for this round of demonstrations.
The CGT trade union, meanwhile, said 800,000 participated in protests across France, with 250,000 people taking part in Paris.
Saturday's protesters were limited by Parisian authorities to the city's southeastern edge, away from the center.
Authorities prepared to help the protesters march safely from the Place d'Italie in the 13th arrondissement on the left bank of the Seine River to Porte de Vincennes which lies further away on the right bank.
A post on X by Paris Police Prefecture showed the Porte d'Italie from the sky ahead of the march.
French news agency AFP reported clashes in Paris after the demonstrations.
French use tear gas at protests in Lyon, Lille, Toulouse and Nantes
The French police used tear gas in response to protests in the southeastern city of Lyon. Use of tear gas was also reported in the cities of Lille, Toulouse and Nantes.
Protests against Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally in Orleans
In Orleans, south of Paris, protesters also came out to the streets against a two-day congress held in the city of Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party.
According to polls, Le Pen is the frontrunner in France's presidential elections next year.

title: Nicki Minaj: Donald Trump lobt ihren Hintern. Wird sie seine neue Sprecherin?
content_c:
US-Präsident Trump lobt Nicki Minajs Hintern. Wird sie seine neue Pressesprecherin?
Donald Trump macht Wahlkampf. In gut einer Woche stehen die US-Kongresswahlen an, und der Präsident tingelt deshalb von Bundesstaat zu Bundesstaat, um die Kandidatinnen und Kandidaten seiner Republikaner zu unterstützen. Am Sonntag reiste er dafür nach Port Huron in Michigan. Im Schlepptau hatte er eine inzwischen bekannte Unterstützerin: die Rapperin Nicki Minaj, 43.
Behalten Sie den Überblick: Jeden Werktag gegen 18 Uhr beantworten SPIEGEL-Autorinnen und -Autoren die wichtigsten Fragen des Tages im Newsletter »Die Lage am Abend« – hintergründig, kompakt, kostenlos. Hier bestellen Sie Ihr News-Briefing als Mail.
Sie stand in Port Huron auf der Bühne und lobte den US-Präsidenten überschwänglich. Der gab das Kompliment kurz darauf zurück – und bezog sich dabei vor allem auf ihr Äußeres. »Übrigens, ich habe mir vorhin einen verdammt schönen Hintern angesehen: den von Nicki Minaj. Den kann man kaum übersehen«, rief er von der Bühne aus, als sie schon wieder im Publikum Platz genommen hatte. Dann fuhr er an sie gewandt fort: »Steh auf. Den kann man kaum übersehen.«
Minaj folgte Trumps Worten und ließ sich stehend vom Publikum beklatschen.
Er hoffe, Minaj sei nicht beleidigt, sagte Trump dann noch. »Aber wir lieben Nicki. Sie ist schon eine ganze Weile bei uns dabei.«
Donald Trump says Nicki Minaj has a “beautiful a**” during rally in Port Huron, Michigan: 
“That’s hard to miss. Stand up” pic.twitter.com/EVbHdDw0t0
Ich bin damit einverstanden, dass mir externe Inhalte angezeigt werden. Damit können personenbezogene Daten an Drittplattformen übermittelt werden. Mehr dazu in unserer Datenschutzerklärung.
Minaj hat sich in der Vergangenheit bereits mehrfach an der Seite Trumps gezeigt (mehr zu der Freundschaft hier ). Für ihren Auftritt in Michigan durfte sie nun auch an Bord des US-Regierungsfliegers »Air Force One«. Der Kommunikationsdirektor des Weißen Hauses, Steven Cheung, postete auf X ein Video , das ihn gemeinsam mit Minaj in dem Flugzeug zeigt. »Meine Damen und Herren, ich glaube, wir haben die neue Pressesprecherin des Weißen Hauses gefunden«, schrieb er dazu.
Der Posten ist tatsächlich frei. Trumps letzte Pressesprecherin, Katie Zacharia, war ihren Job nach fünf Tagen wieder los (mehr dazu hier ).

Minaj als Sprecherin des US-Präsidenten? Das dürfte eher unwahrscheinlich sein. Aber auch Trump-Berater Alex Bruesewitz hat offenbar Spaß an dem Gedankenspiel. Er teilte Cheungs Post auf seinem Account und wandte sich an Minajs Fans, die »Barbz«: »Was halten wir von dieser Idee?«, fragte er.
Der offizielle Account des Weißen Hauses kommentierte Cheungs Nachricht mit dem Zwei-Augen-Emoji: 👀. Und Minaj antwortete schließlich mit zwei Emojis: Sie postete die amerikanische Flagge und das grinsende Gesicht mit Schweißtropfen.

title: Auftakt der RN-Wahlkampagne: Le Pen spricht von "Wiedergeburt" Frankreichs
content_c:
Auftakt der RN-Wahlkampagne Le Pen spricht von "Wiedergeburt" Frankreichs
Die rechtspopulistische französische Präsidentschaftskandidatin Le Pen führt derzeit in den Umfragen. Zum Auftakt der Wahlkampagne ihres Rassemblement National warb sie für einen politischen Neuanfang.
In der ersten großen Rede ihrer Kampagne zur Präsidentschaftswahl hat die rechtspopulistische Politikerin Marine Le Pen für einen politischen Neuanfang Frankreichs plädiert. Unter dem Motto der "Wiedergeburt“ ("Renaissance") sprach sie sich vor den 8.500 Delegierten des Parteitags des Rassemblement National (RN) in Orléans unter anderem gegen Einwanderung aus, die französische Städte "überschwemmt". Auch will sie kriminelle Organisationen bekämpfen.
Sie wolle Frankreich seine "Macht, seine Größe und seine Ausstrahlung" zurückgeben, so wie es am Ende des Mittelalters der Fall gewesen sei, sagte Le Pen. Dabei schlage sie keine Rückkehr in die Vergangenheit, sondern den Beginn einer neuen Ära vor.
Ihre Rede war von Optimismus und Zuversicht geprägt. "Wir werden den öffentlichen Raum schützen, damit er ein Ort des Lebens, der Gelassenheit, des gegenseitigen Respekts bleibt", erklärte Le Pen weiter. Höflichkeit sei der sicherste Weg, "um Gewalt in unserer Gesellschaft zurückzudrängen", sagte Le Pen. "Wir werden wieder an die französische Lebensart anknüpfen, die unser Land einst zum 'lieblichen Frankreich' machte."
Scharfe Kritik an Macron
Nach zehn Jahren unter Amtsinhaber Emmanuel Macron kämen Begriffe wie Ruinen, Niedergang und Unruhen in den Sinn, sagte die 58-Jährige. Sie wolle "den Rechtsstaat wiederherstellen" und Kinder und Familien schützen. Ausländische Straftäter sollten automatisch und konsequent abgeschoben werden. Mit Blick auf mehr Kaufkraft für die Menschen wolle sie Energiesteuern senken.
In der Rentenpolitik forderte sie, dass junge Menschen früher anfangen zu arbeiten. Le Pen betonte zudem, dass sie Soziales nicht gegen Wirtschaft, Rechte nicht gegen Linke ausspielen wolle. Sie griff dazu nach ihren Angaben auf ein Sprichwort zurück: "Ich bin weder der rechte Flügel noch der linke Flügel. Ich bin der Vogel."
Laut Umfragen Favoritin
Die RN-Politikerin kandidiert zum vierten Mal für das Präsidentenamt. Die Wahlen finden im kommenden Frühjahr statt. Umfragen sehen sie derzeit im ersten Wahlgang klar auf dem ersten Platz, auch in der Stichwahl würde sie sich derzeit gegen jeden anderen Kandidaten durchsetzen.
Le Pen betonte, sie werde am nächsten Tag den Vorsitz der RN-Fraktion in der Nationalversammlung niederlegen, um zu unterstreichen, dass sie nicht als Vertreterin einer Partei antrete.
Unruhen bei Rede von Bardella
Die Veranstaltung wurde von Protesten begleitet. 3.000 Sicherheitskräfte waren laut Präfektur im Einsatz. Während der Rede von Le Pens Schützling Jordan Bardella, der aus ihrer Sicht Premierminister werden soll, gab es Unruhen im Publikum. Auf der Plattform X bekannte sich dazu der französische Verband jüdischer Studierender. Bardella sieht sich derzeit nach Medienrecherchen mit schweren Antisemitismusvorwürfen konfrontiert.
Bardella stellte in erster Linie eine harte Ordnungspolitik in Aussicht. "Die Regierung, der ich vorstehen werde, wird alle Mittel nutzen, um Ordnung herzustellen", sagte er. "Polizisten und Gendarmen sind die wichtigsten Schutzschilde der Gesellschaft", betonte er vor dem Hintergrund der jüngsten gewaltsamen Ausschreitungen am Rande von Massenprotesten im ganzen Land.
Bardella kündigte an, er wolle die Strafmündigkeit auf 16 Jahre absenken und zusätzliche Plätze in den Gefängnissen schaffen. "Wer einen Polizisten angreift, schläft noch am selben Abend im Gefängnis." Ausländische Straftäter sollten umgehend abgeschoben werden, die Einwanderung solle insgesamt reduziert werden.

title: На компанию Anthropic подали иск в связи с использованием песен Элвиса Пресли для обучения моделей ИИ
content_c:
Компания Authentic Brands Group подала иск против Anthropic в связи с предполагаемым нарушением прав на 274 песни певца Элвиса Пресли. Правообладатели требуют около 41 миллиона долларов в качестве компенсации. Об этом сообщило издание The Guardian.
Authentic Brands Group, владеющая правами на музыкальный каталог и коммерческое использование образа Элвиса Пресли, обвиняет Anthropic в использовании его песен для обучения систем искусственного интеллекта без согласования. Иск охватывает 274 композиции. Среди них — Can’t Help Falling in Love, All Shook Up и A Little Less Conversation. За каждое произведение, права на которое якобы нарушили, истцы требуют 150 тысяч долларов.
Разработчики искусственного интеллекта уже сталкивались с претензиями Американской ассоциации звукозаписывающих компаний RIAA и крупных музыкальных компаний, в частности Sony, Universal и Warner Records. Новое дело стало одним из первых масштабных исков против разработчика ИИ непосредственно со стороны представителей прав на творческое наследие отдельного исполнителя. Его исход может создать более широкий прецедент для использования имеющихся музыкальных каталогов в системах искусственного интеллекта. Речь идет об условиях, при которых технологические компании могут использовать защищенные произведения для обучения моделей.
«Истцы по делу Элвиса подают этот иск, чтобы обеспечить защиту этих исключительных прав от ответчика, который построил всю свою бизнес-модель на основе нарушения авторских прав в невиданных ранее масштабах», — написал в иске главный адвокат истцов Ричард Буш.
В иске также утверждается, что с самого начала работы Claude генерировал материалы с нарушением прав практически на каждую песню из всех доступных в интернете каталогов. Это утверждение стороны истцов. Отдельные претензии касаются защитных ограничений Claude.
По утверждению правообладателей, Anthropic ввела их после выявления нарушений, чтобы ограничить воспроизведение защищенных музыкальных произведений. Однако эти меры предосторожности, как указано в иске, оказались неэффективными. Истцы считают, что компания знала о недостатках ограничений, но продолжала допускать нарушения. По их мнению, это свидетельствует о сознательном характере действий Anthropic.
Музыкальные ИИ-платформы обучаются на больших массивах записанной музыки. Они анализируют звучание, структуру композиций и особенности музыкального выражения. После этого пользователи могут создавать новые сгенерированные треки по текстовым или голосовым запросам. Именно использование существующих произведений для обучения таких систем остается предметом споров между технологическими компаниями и музыкальной индустрией.
Музыканты неоднократно выражали опасения по поводу использования их песен и голосов без разрешения. Их также беспокоит перспектива вытеснения человеческого творчества массовым потоком сгенерированных композиций. Часть такого контента называют «AI slop» из-за его низкого качества и большого объема. Кроме того, на музыкальных стриминговых платформах уже появились ИИ-боты, которые выдают себя за реальных современных исполнителей.
На прошлой неделе Spotify сообщил об ограничении распространения такого контента. По заявлению сервиса, в течение прошлого года из рекомендаций для пользователей удалили около 50 миллионов песен, которые признали низкокачественной ИИ-музыкой. Это решение касалось рекомендаций, благодаря которым слушатели открывают для себя новые композиции.
Напомним, что защиты контента от использования ИИ без разрешения добиваются и участники коалиции SPUR. 12 октября к ней присоединились The New York Times, AFP и The Economist. После расширения объединение насчитывает более 80 участников из более чем 20 стран. Коалиция разрабатывает стандарты и технические системы для отслеживания использования материалов и заключения лицензионных соглашений.
Кроме того, в августе Sony Music и Warner Music подали иск против Anthropic из-за предполагаемого использования десятков тысяч музыкальных произведений для обучения Claude. Компании утверждают, что защищенные произведения получали через торренты, автоматизированный сбор данных и загрузку. Они требуют предусмотренных законом компенсаций за каждое нарушение, что потенциально может обернуться многомиллиардными выплатами. Anthropic отвергла эти претензии и заявила о намерении защищаться в суде.
description: Истцы требуют по 150 тысяч долларов за каждое произведение, которое якобы было использовано без их согласия.
content:
Компания Authentic Brands Group подала иск против Anthropic в связи с предполагаемым нарушением прав на 274 песни певца Элвиса Пресли. Правообладатели требуют около 41 миллиона долларов в качестве компенсации. Об этом сообщило издание The Guardian.
Authentic Brands Group, владеющая правами на музыкальный каталог и коммерческое использование образа Элвиса Пресли, обвиняет Anthropic в использовании его песен для обучения систем искусственного интеллекта без согласования. Иск охватывает 274 композиции. Среди них — Can’t Help Falling in Love, All Shook Up и A Little Less Conversation. За каждое произведение, права на которое якобы нарушили, истцы требуют 150 тысяч долларов.
Разработчики искусственного интеллекта уже сталкивались с претензиями Американской ассоциации звукозаписывающих компаний RIAA и крупных музыкальных компаний, в частности Sony, Universal и Warner Records. Новое дело стало одним из первых масштабных исков против разработчика ИИ непосредственно со стороны представителей прав на творческое наследие отдельного исполнителя. Его исход может создать более широкий прецедент для использования имеющихся музыкальных каталогов в системах искусственного интеллекта. Речь идет об условиях, при которых технологические компании могут использовать защищенные произведения для обучения моделей.
«Истцы по делу Элвиса подают этот иск, чтобы обеспечить защиту этих исключительных прав от ответчика, который построил всю свою бизнес-модель на основе нарушения авторских прав в невиданных ранее масштабах», — написал в иске главный адвокат истцов Ричард Буш.
В иске также утверждается, что с самого начала работы Claude генерировал материалы с нарушением прав практически на каждую песню из всех доступных в интернете каталогов. Это утверждение стороны истцов. Отдельные претензии касаются защитных ограничений Claude.
По утверждению правообладателей, Anthropic ввела их после выявления нарушений, чтобы ограничить воспроизведение защищенных музыкальных произведений. Однако эти меры предосторожности, как указано в иске, оказались неэффективными. Истцы считают, что компания знала о недостатках ограничений, но продолжала допускать нарушения. По их мнению, это свидетельствует о сознательном характере действий Anthropic.
Музыкальные ИИ-платформы обучаются на больших массивах записанной музыки. Они анализируют звучание, структуру композиций и особенности музыкального выражения. После этого пользователи могут создавать новые сгенерированные треки по текстовым или голосовым запросам. Именно использование существующих произведений для обучения таких систем остается предметом споров между технологическими компаниями и музыкальной индустрией.
Музыканты неоднократно выражали опасения по поводу использования их песен и голосов без разрешения. Их также беспокоит перспектива вытеснения человеческого творчества массовым потоком сгенерированных композиций. Часть такого контента называют «AI slop» из-за его низкого качества и большого объема. title: Вучич визнав поразку правлячої партії на парламентських виборах у Сербії на користь студентського руху – ЗМІ
content_c:
Лідер правлячої Сербської прогресивної партії (SNS) та кандидат на посаду прем'єр-міністра Александар Вучич визнав поразку своєї політсили на позачергових парламентських виборах у неділю, поступившись опозиційному студентському протестному руху, повідомляє агентство Reuters.
"У нас ще немає остаточних результатів, але на основі вибірки... зрозуміло, що ми програли ці вибори. Студентський список переміг: вони матимуть від 135 до 140 місць, а ми – 105, більше ніхто до парламенту не пройшов", – заявив Вучич журналістам.
Позачергові вибори були призначені Вучичем у вересні після майже двох років безперервних студентських протестів проти корупції та посилення авторитаризму влади. Демонстрації спалахнули після трагедії у місті Новий Сад у 2024 році, де внаслідок обвалу навісу на залізничному вокзалі загинуло 16 людей.
Студентський рух здобув широку суспільну підтримку та став найбільшим політичним викликом для Вучича від моменту його приходу до влади на посаду прем'єр-міністра у 2014 році та подальшого обрання президентом у 2017 році.

title: Gabon says access to social media restored after eight-month ban
content_c:
Gabon says access to social media restored after eight-month ban
- Published
Gabon says it has lifted a ban on social media imposed eight months ago - a move that triggered widespread criticism at the time.
The High Communication Authority (HAC) announced the U-turn on Saturday in a televised statement. The BBC has approached the country's media regulator for comment.
The ban had been introduced on 17 February, with the HAC saying that online content was fuelling conflict and deepening divisions in the country.
The move came as a shock to the central African nation of about 2.5 million people, where social media platforms such as Facebook, TikTok, YouTube and Instagram have been particularly popular with younger people who use it for business as well as pleasure.
Many turned to VPNs in order to continue accessing social media sites following the ban.
The ban had been imposed at a time when the Gabonese President Brice Oligui Nguema was facing a wave of social unrest less than a year after his election.
Teachers and civil servants had staged strikes over what they said were low pay and poor working conditions.
The opposition said the suspension was an abuse of power.
Nguema won last year's elections with more than 90% of the vote, two years after his coup had ended more than five decades of rule by the Bongo family.
At the time he pledged to reform Gabon, a small, oil- and timber-rich country, where digital blackouts were used by the previous governments to control information.

title: Australia politics live: Zali Steggall accuses Angus Taylor of not ‘reading the room’ in Haines tribute speech
content_c:
The independent MP, who sits next to Haines in the lower house, said “there is a link between our words and actions”.
At a press conference shortly before question time, Steggall said:
I did not feel that Angus Taylor read the room when it comes to the lesson that Helen would like us all to learn. To make what’s happened to her, the utter tragedy of it, make sense to all of us, makes sense for Australia, then we have to be able to take responsibility for the impact our words and our debate has beyond the walls of Parliament. And the same goes to the words and the images and the editorials used in media, social media ... what ads we authorise at election time for a party.
These were all part of Phil [Haines]’s speech to us this morning, his words to us, asking us to raise the bar so that when Helen does come back to this place, there’s been a meaningful shift in how we can have a respectful debate.
We can disagree respectfully, but words matter and have an impact.
Canavan rejects idea that Haines attack marks ‘turning point’ in political discourse
Nationals leader Matt Canavan has pushed back against suggestions that the attack on independent MP Helen Haines marks a “turning point” in Australian politics.
Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Canavan dismissed the suggestion that rhetoric in Canberra has deteriorated, describing parliament as a “release valve” for society.
“I don’t particularly think our political rhetoric is overly different from eras gone past,” he said.
Following Andrew Hastie’s call to leave “the ‘nasty personal politics of Maga” politics behind in the wake of the attack on Haines, Canavan rejected any direct link between a political commentary and community violence. He also pushed back against calls for politicians to receive increase security.
Police officers, emergency officers, nurses face probably more constant threats of assault and real physical challenges than we do…
I’m not asking for any kind of special protection here.
Canavan added that he was “a little bit wary” of a proposed parliamentary civility pledge, saying:
If we go too far the other way, that’ll actually increase tensions and reduce social harmony.
Ryan hits out at ‘tone deaf’ Taylor comments after Haines attack
Following parliament’s tributes to Helen Haines, the independent MP Monique Ryan has said that politicians must change their conduct in the wake of the “unthinkable” attack on her crossbench colleague.
Appearing on the ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Ryan said political leaders should listen to security experts who correlate the tone of political language with rising community aggression.
She criticised the opposition leader Angus Taylor’s speech paying tribute to Haines this morning as “tone deaf” and “hugely disappointing”, particularly in light of remarks made by Haines’s husband earlier in the day.
If Angus Taylor doesn’t think that the words that we use matter, I don’t understand how he aspires to lead a political party …
If we can’t rise to the occasion now after something as unthinkable as what happened to Helen and think about how we behave in the house and in the public space … we’re never going to do that.
First international flight touches down at Western Sydney airport
Western Sydney airport welcomed its first international passengers this morning, after Air New Zealand flight NZ165 touched down.
The arrival marks the start of commercial international services at the new airport – Australia’s first major new airport in more than 50 years.
Following a brief turnaround, the return flight (NZ166) departed fully booked. Air New Zealand will operate three return flights weekly on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays.
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, welcomed the arrival as a milestone for the area:
Western Sydney is now connected directly to the world, bringing more jobs, more visitors and more opportunities for local businesses.
And importantly, it means people in Western Sydney can fly overseas without having to travel across the city first.
Big Build royal commission to hold public hearings through much of the Victorian election campaign
The royal commission into allegations of corruption on Victorian government construction sites is set to hold two weeks of public hearings in the middle of the state election campaign.
The inquiry updated its website on Monday afternoon confirming the first block of public hearings from 9 November to 20 November.
This falls during the caretaker period, when the election campaign is expected to be in full swing, and includes a few days of early voting, which opens on 18 November.
Labor MPs are bracing for potentially damaging allegations.
Here’s what the royal commisison heard on the first public hearing last month:
Government accused of ignoring lessons from robodebt
An algorithm used by the federal government to assess the level of care older Australians are entitled to is unreasonable, unfair and lacks human oversight, according to a damning investigation by the commonwealth ombudsman.
The investigation also found transparency recommendations from the robodebt royal commission have been ignored.
The investigation followed reporting by Guardian Australia that older people were being left distressed and without adequate care after their home support needs were assessed by an “inhumane” algorithm as part of the government’s mandatory Integrated Assessment Tool (IAT).
Aged care assessors are barred from overriding the IAT’s funding package recommendation, even when the decision is wrong.
Documents released under freedom of information reveal departmental panic, severe clinical distress among frontline assessors, and secret IT workarounds after officials realised in the hours before the rollout of the algorithm that legislation legally barred human override, and that this was causing distress within days of implementation.
The shadow health minister, Anne Ruston,said the report shows: “The algorithm must be scrapped.”
Labor defended this system for months while the Coalition and the crossbench said it was broken. Today the independent umpire has agreed with us.
NSW police minister says gun buyback reflective of ‘very sensible approach’ by government
The NSW police minister, Yasmin Catley, and police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, held a press conference earlier today to detail the state’s gun buyback program. As we reported earlier, eligible licence holders are now able to book an appointment to surrender any excess or reclassified firearms from next Monday, 2 November.
Catley said bookings were essential as the buyback program began, saying people cannot walk into police stations without an appointment. Those who do turn in eligible weapons will receive compensation ranging from $450 to $1,000, depending on the firearm. Small businesses affected by changes to gun laws will also be eligible for grants up to $25,000.
A second phase for high-value firearms will begin next year.
“This has been a very sensible approach by the government,” she told reporters.
A very sensitive way of responding to the worst terrorist attack that we have seen on our streets in this country.
When asked about a draft proposal to allow some to apply for more than 10 firearms in limited circumstances, Catley said people would need “a very good reason”, such as competitive sport shooting.
“If you are at those elite levels, then it may be the case that you do need more than the 10 guns,” she said.
The independent MP, who sits next to Haines in the lower house, said “there is a link between our words and actions”.
At a press conference shortly before question time, Steggall said:
I did not feel that Angus Taylor read the room when it comes to the lesson that Helen would like us all to learn. To make what’s happened to her, the utter tragedy of it, make sense to all of us, makes sense for Australia, then we have to be able to take responsibility for the impact our words and our debate has beyond the walls of Parliament. And the same goes to the words and the images and the editorials used in media, social media ... what ads we authorise at election time for a party.
These were all part of Phil [Haines]’s speech to us this morning, his words to us, asking us to raise the bar so that when Helen does come back to this place, there’s been a meaningful shift in how we can have a respectful debate.
We can disagree respectfully, but words matter and have an impact.
The alleged attack on independent MP Helen Haines loomed large over the House of Representatives, creating a civil yet sombre question time. Some politicians offered compliments to their counterparts across the aisle, others contributed by keeping their derision for dixers to themselves.
The government faced questions on the sale of Victoria Barracks in Sydney.
The impact of social media on violence against women, workers and politicians came under the spotlight.
There were no ejections and just one warning.
It is yet to be seen whether this question time atmosphere will last more than one day.
Helen Haines granted leave of absence until at least end of sitting year
The independent MP for Indi, Helen Haines, has been given leave of absence until 26 November after she was injured in an alleged attack in her electorate.
The leader of the House of Representatives, Tony Burke, clarified he had simply chosen the last sitting date of the year:
Obviously, we will continue to move resolutions for as long as Helen needs us to.
No leave of absence motion stops the fact that, if at any moment, Helen feels she’s ready to come, then obviously she immediately will.
Continuing from the previous post, social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, says the tenor of public debate has changed significantly during her three-decade long political career.
It is more violent in its tone, and I think the industrial scale of the abuse that all of us receive – but particularly the women here receive – that has changed.
It’s been supercharged by social media.
But I’d say this about social media … Social media companies profit by the division they drive in our society.
And that’s why all of us have a responsibility to resist that too. To resist that division, to resist the violence and discourse, that the big tech giants are forcing on us.
Tanya Plibersek is asked if public life is safe for women
Independent for Bradfield and the electorate’s first female MP, Nicolette Boele, directs a question to the longest-serving female member of the House of Representatives, Tanya Plibersek.
Boele says:
Violence against women, whether physical, spoken, or in writing, is used to silence them. And when it keeps women out of this place, it decides to represent us. That is not democracy.
What does the minister say to the young women of Australia now, wondering whether public life is safe for them?
Plibersek responds:
I’m not surprised if there are young women all over Australia looking at the horrific [alleged] attack on Helen Haines, and wondering whether a life in public is worth it, whether it’s safe for them.
And what I would say to them is 100% it is worth it.
Every single day in this place, we make important decisions that change this country and change it for the better.
We can’t vacate the field to the people who would stop us from doing that.
Greens leader expects Steele-John to remain on leave until investigation complete
Greens leader David Shoebridge says he’s “glad” Jordon Steele-John made the decision to stay away from Senate estimates after a week of confusion following the release of a letter accusing him of inappropriate behaviour.
Over the weekend, Steele-John said he would not attend parliament next week after seven members wrote to Shoebridge urging an investigation into claims he had acted inappropriately towards women between 2017 and 2025.
Shortly after the letter’s release to parts of the media, Shoebridge said Steele-John would go on leave while an independent investigation took place. Steele-John publicly rejected the idea that he was on leave.
In a press conference before question time this afternoon, Shoebridge said other members of the Greens will ask questions of the departments and agencies involved in the NDIS when they appear later this week. He added he would not go into a “blow-by-blow discussion about the exchanges”.
Asked whether Steele-John would remain on leave until the investigation is complete, Shoebridge responded:
Well, I’ve made it very clear to Senator Steele-John what I believe the community expectations are. If you ask me tomorrow, I’ll say the same. If you ask me the day after it, I’ll say the same. I’ve made it very clear what I believe the community expectations are.
Online radicalisation involves mixed ideologies, with violence the ‘only principle’, Burke says
Home affairs minister, Tony Burke, is asked a dixer on how the government is working with neighbours and partners to keep Australians safe.
He says all countries are now dealing with the radicalisation of young people:
Every country is reporting a new cohort, and growing fast, of young people, particularly male, where we used to worry about people becoming involved and radicalised in their teens.
The radicalisation [is] happening online and involving mixed ideologies.
Ideologies that would be completely incoherent with each other, but only having violence together as their only principle.
I want to assure the House of the cooperative work that Australia is doing with all of our agencies and all of our effort.

Continue reading...
author: Ima Caldwell (now) and Kat Wong (earlier)
content:
The independent MP, who sits next to Haines in the lower house, said “there is a link between our words and actions”.
At a press conference shortly before question time, Steggall said:
I did not feel that Angus Taylor read the room when it comes to the lesson that Helen would like us all to learn. To make what’s happened to her, the utter tragedy of it, make sense to all of us, makes sense for Australia, then we have to be able to take responsibility for the impact our words and our debate has beyond the walls of Parliament. And the same goes to the words and the images and the editorials used in media, social media ... what ads we authorise at election time for a party.
These were all part of Phil [Haines]’s speech to us this morning, his words to us, asking us to raise the bar so that when Helen does come back to this place, there’s been a meaningful shift in how we can have a respectful debate.
We can disagree respectfully, but words matter and have an impact.
Canavan rejects idea that Haines attack marks ‘turning point’ in political discourse
Nationals leader Matt Canavan has pushed back against suggestions that the attack on independent MP Helen Haines marks a “turning point” in Australian politics.
Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Canavan dismissed the suggestion that rhetoric in Canberra has deteriorated, describing parliament as a “release valve” for society.
“I don’t particularly think our political rhetoric is overly different from eras gone past,” he said.
Following Andrew Hastie’s call to leave “the ‘nasty personal politics of Maga” politics behind in the wake of the attack on Haines, Canavan rejected any direct link between a political commentary and community violence. He also pushed back against calls for politicians to receive increase security.
Police officers, emergency officers, nurses face probably more constant threats of assault and real physical challenges than we do…
I’m not asking for any kind of special protection here.
Canavan added that he was “a little bit wary” of a proposed parliamentary civility pledge, saying:
If we go too far the other way, that’ll actually increase tensions and reduce social harmony.
Ryan hits out at ‘tone deaf’ Taylor comments after Haines attack
Following parliament’s tributes to Helen Haines, the independent MP Monique Ryan has said that politicians must change their conduct in the wake of the “unthinkable” attack on her crossbench colleague.
Appearing on the ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Ryan said political leaders should listen to security experts who correlate the tone of political language with rising community aggression.
She criticised the opposition leader Angus Taylor’s speech paying tribute to Haines this morning as “tone deaf” and “hugely disappointing”, particularly in light of remarks made by Haines’s husband earlier in the day.
If Angus Taylor doesn’t think that the words that we use matter, I don’t understand how he aspires to lead a political party …
If we can’t rise to the occasion now after something as unthinkable as what happened to Helen and think about how we behave in the house and in the public space … we’re never going to do that.
First international flight touches down at Western Sydney airport
Western Sydney airport welcomed its first international passengers this morning, after Air New Zealand flight NZ165 touched down.
The arrival marks the start of commercial international services at the new airport – Australia’s first major new airport in more than 50 years.
Following a brief turnaround, the return flight (NZ166) departed fully booked. Air New Zealand will operate three return flights weekly on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays.
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, welcomed the arrival as a milestone for the area:
Western Sydney is now connected directly to the world, bringing more jobs, more visitors and more opportunities for local businesses.
And importantly, it means people in Western Sydney can fly overseas without having to travel across the city first.
Big Build royal commission to hold public hearings through much of the Victorian election campaign
The royal commission into allegations of corruption on Victorian government construction sites is set to hold two weeks of public hearings in the middle of the state election campaign.
The inquiry updated its website on Monday afternoon confirming the first block of public hearings from 9 November to 20 November.
This falls during the caretaker period, when the election campaign is expected to be in full swing, and includes a few days of early voting, which opens on 18 November.
Labor MPs are bracing for potentially damaging allegations.
Here’s what the royal commisison heard on the first public hearing last month:
Government accused of ignoring lessons from robodebt
An algorithm used by the federal government to assess the level of care older Australians are entitled to is unreasonable, unfair and lacks human oversight, according to a damning investigation by the commonwealth ombudsman.
The investigation also found transparency recommendations from the robodebt royal commission have been ignored.
The investigation followed reporting by Guardian Australia that older people were being left distressed and without adequate care after their home support needs were assessed by an “inhumane” algorithm as part of the government’s mandatory Integrated Assessment Tool (IAT).
Aged care assessors are barred from overriding the IAT’s funding package recommendation, even when the decision is wrong.
Documents released under freedom of information reveal departmental panic, severe clinical distress among frontline assessors, and secret IT workarounds after officials realised in the hours before the rollout of the algorithm that legislation legally barred human override, and that this was causing distress within days of implementation.
The shadow health minister, Anne Ruston,said the report shows: “The algorithm must be scrapped.”
Labor defended this system for months while the Coalition and the crossbench said it was broken. Today the independent umpire has agreed with us.
NSW police minister says gun buyback reflective of ‘very sensible approach’ by government
The NSW police minister, Yasmin Catley, and police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, held a press conference earlier today to detail the state’s gun buyback program. As we reported earlier, eligible licence holders are now able to book an appointment to surrender any excess or reclassified firearms from next Monday, 2 November.
Catley said bookings were essential as the buyback program began, saying people cannot walk into police stations without an appointment. Those who do turn in eligible weapons will receive compensation ranging from $450 to $1,000, depending on the firearm. Small businesses affected by changes to gun laws will also be eligible for grants up to $25,000.
A second phase for high-value firearms will begin next year.
“This has been a very sensible approach by the government,” she told reporters.
A very sensitive way of responding to the worst terrorist attack that we have seen on our streets in this country.
When asked about a draft proposal to allow some to apply for more than 10 firearms in limited circumstances, Catley said people would need “a very good reason”, such as competitive sport shooting.
“If you are at those elite levels, then it may be the case that you do need more than the 10 guns,” she said.
The independent MP, who sits next to Haines in the lower house, said “there is a link between our words and actions”.
At a press conference shortly before question time, Steggall said:
I did not feel that Angus Taylor read the room when it comes to the lesson that Helen would like us all to learn. To make what’s happened to her, the utter tragedy of it, make sense to all of us, makes sense for Australia, then we have to be able to take responsibility for the impact our words and our debate has beyond the walls of Parliament. And the same goes to the words and the images and the editorials used in media, social media ... what ads we authorise at election time for a party.
These were all part of Phil [Haines]’s speech to us this morning, his words to us, asking us to raise the bar so that when Helen does come back to this place, there’s been a meaningful shift in how we can have a respectful debate.
We can disagree respectfully, but words matter and have an impact.
The alleged attack on independent MP Helen Haines loomed large over the House of Representatives, creating a civil yet sombre question time. Some politicians offered compliments to their counterparts across the aisle, others contributed by keeping their derision for dixers to themselves.
The government faced questions on the sale of Victoria Barracks in Sydney.
The impact of social media on violence against women, workers and politicians came under the spotlight.
There were no ejections and just one warning.
It is yet to be seen whether this question time atmosphere will last more than one day.
Helen Haines granted leave of absence until at least end of sitting year
The independent MP for Indi, Helen Haines, has been given leave of absence until 26 November after she was injured in an alleged attack in her electorate.
The leader of the House of Representatives, Tony Burke, clarified he had simply chosen the last sitting date of the year:
Obviously, we will continue to move resolutions for as long as Helen needs us to.
No leave of absence motion stops the fact that, if at any moment, Helen feels she’s ready to come, then obviously she immediately will.
Continuing from the previous post, social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, says the tenor of public debate has changed significantly during her three-decade long political career.
It is more violent in its tone, and I think the industrial scale of the abuse that all of us receive – but particularly the women here receive – that has changed.
It’s been supercharged by social media.
But I’d say this about social media … Social media companies profit by the division they drive in our society.
And that’s why all of us have a responsibility to resist that too. To resist that division, to resist the violence and discourse, that the big tech giants are forcing on us.
Tanya Plibersek is asked if public life is safe for women
Independent for Bradfield and the electorate’s first female MP, Nicolette Boele, directs a question to the longest-serving female member of the House of Representatives, Tanya Plibersek.
Boele says:
Violence against women, whether physical, spoken, or in writing, is used to silence them. And when it keeps women out of this place, it decides to represent us. That is not democracy.
What does the minister say to the young women of Australia now, wondering whether public life is safe for them?
Plibersek responds:
I’m not surprised if there are young women all over Australia looking at the horrific [alleged] attack on Helen Haines, and wondering whether a life in public is worth it, whether it’s safe for them.
And what I would say to them is 100% it is worth it.
Every single day in this place, we make important decisions that change this country and change it for the better.
We can’t vacate the field to the people who would stop us from doing that.
Greens leader expects Steele-John to remain on leave until investigation complete
Greens leader David Shoebridge says he’s “glad” Jordon Steele-John made the decision to stay away from Senate estimates after a week of confusion following the release of a letter accusing him of inappropriate behaviour.
Over the weekend, Steele-John said he would not attend parliament next week after seven members wrote to Shoebridge urging an investigation into claims he had acted inappropriately towards women between 2017 and 2025.
Shortly after the letter’s release to parts of the media, Shoebridge said Steele-John would go on leave while an independent investigation took place. Steele-John publicly rejected the idea that he was on leave.
In a press conference before question time this afternoon, Shoebridge said other members of the Greens will ask questions of the departments and agencies involved in the NDIS when they appear later this week. He added he would not go into a “blow-by-blow discussion about the exchanges”.
Asked whether Steele-John would remain on leave until the investigation is complete, Shoebridge responded:
Well, I’ve made it very clear to Senator Steele-John what I believe the community expectations are. If you ask me tomorrow, I’ll say the same. If you ask me the day after it, I’ll say the same. I’ve made it very clear what I believe the community expectations are.
Online radicalisation involves mixed ideologies, with violence the ‘only principle’, Burke says
Home affairs minister, Tony Burke, is asked a dixer on how the government is working with neighbours and partners to keep Australians safe.
He says all countries are now dealing with the radicalisation of young people:
Every country is reporting a new cohort, and growing fast, of young people, particularly male, where we used to worry about people becoming involved and radicalised in their teens.
The radicalisation [is] happening online and involving mixed ideologies.
Ideologies that would be completely incoherent with each other, but only having violence together as their only principle.
I want to assure the House of the cooperative work that Australia is doing with all of our agencies and all of our effort.

title: Brazil votes in tight runoff between leftist Lula and right-wing Flavio Bolsonaro
content_c:
Brazil votes in tight runoff between Lula and Bolsonaro
Published October 25, 2026last updated October 25, 2026
Voters in Brazil headed to the polls on Sunday for a presidential runoff election between incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro.
In the first round earlier this month, Bolsonaro surpassed Lula by more than 2.2 million votes. More than 33 million voters out of nearly 160 million abstained.
However, Sunday's runoff election is expected to be neck-and-neck, with recent polls showing Lula closing the gap.
Candidates need more than 50% of the vote to become president.
Election to determine Brazil's direction
The high-stakes election is set to determine Brazil's political direction, pitting left-of-center veteran Lula, 80, against right-wing Bolsonaro, 45, who is an ally of the US.
If Bolsonaro wins, it will signify a shift to the right for Brazil and could determine the extent to which the US will be able to grow its influence in Latin America.
Lula has campaigned to continue his social policies to boost employment and reduce poverty, while Bolsonaro has pledged a tougher course against crime and a political fresh start.
Flavio has also pledged to free his father, who is under house arrest for attempting a coup in 2022, if he is elected.
However, if Lula, who has opposed the US President Donald Trump over trade and security, secures a fourth term, it is likely to pose hurdles for Washington.
The 80-year-old was previously head of state from 2003 to 2010, and became president again in 2023.
Flavio Bolsonaro has sat in the Senate since 2019 and is running for the presidency for the first time.
The rematch between Lula and Bolsonaro comes against the backdrop of corruption scandals, economic downslide and accusations of US interference, which Washington denies.
Around 159 million people are eligible to vote in the election.
Preliminary results are expected on Sunday night.
Edited by: Natalie Muller

title: Libyen – USA: Libyen bestellt US-Vertreter wegen Trumps Hetze ein
content_c:
Verbalattacke aus D.C. Libyen bestellt wegen Trumps Hetze den Leiter der US-Vertretung ein
Verbale Breitseiten des US-Präsidenten gegen andere (oft ärmere Länder) sind nichts Neues. Nicht ganz so oft kommt es allerdings vor, dass die so herabgewürdigten Länder dagegenhalten. Nun aber hat das libysche Außenministerium den Leiter der US-Vertretung einbestellt.
Zuvor hatte die Behörde öffentliche Äußerungen von Donald Trump gegenüber Libyen als beleidigend bezeichnet. Das Ministerium weise alle Erklärungen zurück, die die Würde des libyschen Volkes herabsetzten, hieß es in einer Mitteilung.
Sowohl die Regierung im Westen als auch die rivalisierende Führung im Osten des Landes verurteilten Trumps Aussagen. Sie wiesen zudem Versuche zurück, Libyen in US-Wahlkampfdebatten hineinzuziehen.
Trump hatte am Samstag bei einem Auftritt im US-Bundesstaat Georgia den US-Senator Jon Ossoff verbal angegriffen. Dieser habe persönlich einen Gesetzentwurf eingebracht, um »Armeen von Migranten aus terrorverseuchten Ländern wie Libyen, dem Jemen, Haiti und Somalia« ins Land zu holen, sagte Trump. »Erinnert ihr euch, wie ich sie genannt habe? Dreckslochländer«, fügte er in Anspielung auf Äußerungen während seiner ersten Amtszeit hinzu.
Am Sonntagabend wurde Trump dann auf seiner Onlineplattform Truth Social versöhnlich und erklärte, die USA fühlten sich den Beziehungen zu Libyen verpflichtet. Das libysche Volk sei stolz, widerstandsfähig und gastfreundlich. »Wir respektieren das libysche Volk und die Opfer, die mutige Libyer im Kampf gegen die IS-Miliz, den gemeinsamen Feind unserer beiden Völker, gebracht haben«, schrieb Trump. Er fügte jedoch hinzu, dass Libyen kein Korridor für illegale Migration bleiben dürfe und dies sofort enden müsse.
Immer wieder geht es gegen Somalia
Rassistische und menschenverachtende Aussagen des amtierenden US-Präsidenten hat es in der Vergangenheit schon öfter gegeben. Legendär war seine Bezeichnung von Haiti und mehreren afrikanischen Staaten als »Dreckslöcher« (»shithole countries«) im Jahr 2018. An dieser Denkweise scheint sich wenig geändert zu haben, wie die jüngste verbale Entgleisung nahelegt.
Trump hat zudem Ende Dezember 2025 Migranten aus Somalia für unerwünscht erklärt und als »Müll« bezeichnet. »Ihr Land stinkt, und wir wollen sie nicht in unserem Land«, sagte Trump damals bei einer Kabinettssitzung in Washington. Das englische Wort »stinks« lässt sich dabei wörtlich, also als übel riechend, übersetzen. Es kann aber auch im übertragenen Sinne als »Ihr Land taugt nichts« gemeint sein. »Wir gehen in die falsche Richtung, wenn wir weiterhin Müll in unser Land aufnehmen«, sagte Trump zur geplanten Verschärfung der Aufenthaltsregeln.
description: »Terrorverseucht« und« Dreckslochland«: Diese Beschimpfungen des US-Präsidenten wollte man sich in Libyen nicht gefallen lassen – und ließ die Sache diplomatisch eskalieren. Später gab sich Donald Trump dann plötzlich handzahm.

title: Stromsteuer-Debatte: Union und SPD weiter weit auseinander
content_c:
Bericht aus Berlin Union und SPD bei Stromsteuer-Debatte weiter weit auseinander
Dass Unternehmen und Haushalte beim Strompreis entlastet werden sollen, darüber herrscht in der Regierung Einigkeit. Unklar aber ist, wie das finanziert werden kann. Im Bericht aus Berlin machten CDU und SPD sehr unterschiedliche Vorschläge.
Europa erlebt in diesen Tagen wütende Proteste - am kommenden Wochenende soll auch in Deutschland demonstriert werden. Der Grund: die zuletzt stark gestiegenen Lebenshaltungskosten. Die Politik ist alarmiert und hat versprochen, die Bürger schnell zu entlasten. Unklar ist aber nach wie vor, wie genau das in welchem Umfang passieren soll.
Ein Baustein - und Streitpunkt - ist die Stromsteuer. Politiker von SPD und Union haben sich dafür ausgesprochen - zuletzt Kanzler Friedrich Merz am Samstag auf dem Parteitag der CSU. "Wenn es eben geht - und ich denke, es geht - dann muss die Stromsteuer im nächsten Jahr runter", sagte der CDU-Vorsitzende.
Anders sieht dies allerdings Bundesfinanzminister und SPD-Chef Lars Klingbeil. Auch er ist zwar grundsätzlich für eine solche Entlastung, fragt aber, wie das gegenfinanziert werden soll. Denn dem Haushalt würden durch die Steuersenkung am Ende wohl bis zu sechs Milliarden Euro fehlen. "Wir können nichts versprechen, was man am Ende nicht halten kann", stellt Klingbeil klar.
Kretschmer: Parteiübergreifender Ansatz nötig
Im Bericht aus Berlin macht Sachsens Ministerpräsident Michael Kretschmer die schwarz-rote Koalition im Bund für das Finanzierungsdilemma verantwortlich: "Man sieht eben, wie schwierig das ist, wenn man den Anfang einer Regierungszeit verstolpert. Das ist passiert", sagte der CDU-Politiker. Die großen Themen wie etwa die Deregulierung seien nicht angegangen worden - daher brauche man nun so viel Geld.
Kretschmer verwies auf die gemeinsame Forderung der Ministerpräsidenten nach günstigerem Strom. "Wir haben gesagt: Wenn wir wirtschaftliche Leistungsfähigkeit erhalten wollen, muss dieser Schritt kommen." Daher müsse man jetzt zum Beispiel über den Zertifikatehandel oder über die von Wirtschaftsministerin Katherina Reiche im sogenannten Netzpaket vorgeschlagenen Maßnahmen reden. Deutschland verliere sonst den Anschluss.
Dafür brauche es einen parteiübergreifenden Ansatz. "Jeder muss etwas geben." Aber jeder müsse dann auch etwas zurückbekommen. Die Bundesregierung täte gut daran, auf die Ländervertreter zu hören. "Wir haben in vielen Punkten immer wieder früher erkannt, was notwendig ist. Wir haben Recht behalten", so Kretschmer. Die Steuermehreinnahmen 2027 gäben Finanzminister Klingbeil auch den notwendigen Spielraum für die Senkung der Stromsteuer.
Bovenschulte will die Mineralölkonzerne zur Kasse bitten
Ganz anders sieht das Kretschmers Kollege Andreas Bovenschulte von der SPD. Der Bremer Bürgermeister will eine Senkung der Stromsteuer vor allem über eine Übergewinnsteuer für Mineralölkonzerne gegenfinanzieren - ein Vorhaben, das bei der Union nicht auf Gegenliebe stößt. Die Konzerne hätten in der Krise massive Gewinne in Milliardenhöhe abgeschöpft. "Lasst uns endlich denen in die Tasche greifen, die vorher den Bürgerinnen und Bürgern in die Tasche gegriffen haben", forderte Bovenschulte.
Zwar gebe es bislang dafür ohne die Union keine Mehrheit, räumte der SPD-Politiker ein. Aber er habe es noch nicht aufgegeben, die CDU von einer Übergewinnsteuer zu überzeugen. "Ich kann es nicht verstehen, warum sich die Union dieser vernünftigen Lösung versperrt." Zuletzt habe auch der Generalanwalt beim Europäischen Gerichtshof erklärt, dass er eine Übergewinnsteuer für zulässig halte, sagte Bovenschulte mit Blick auf juristische Bedenken in der Union.
Zudem reiche eine Entlastung beim Strompreis nicht aus, so der SPD-Politiker. "Wir brauchen eine Einkommenssteuerreform, die die kleinen und mittleren Einkommen entlastet." Zu einer vernünftigen Gegenfinanzierung gehöre auch, "dass diejenigen, die tatsächlich mehr leisten können, auch ihren Beitrag dazu leisten". Der Staat habe viele aktuell teure Aufgaben - da kann es nicht sein, "dass man immer nur die kleinen Leute auffordert, den Gürtel enger zu schnallen".

Anders sieht dies allerdings Bundesfinanzminister und SPD-Chef Lars Klingbeil. Auch er ist zwar grundsätzlich für eine solche Entlastung, fragt aber, wie das gegenfinanziert werden soll. Denn dem Haushalt würden durch die Steuersenkung am Ende wohl bis zu sechs Milliarden Euro fehlen. "Wir können nichts versprechen, was man am Ende nicht halten kann", stellt Klingbeil klar.
Kretschmer: Parteiübergreifender Ansatz nötig
Im Bericht aus Berlin macht Sachsens Ministerpräsident Michael Kretschmer die schwarz-rote Koalition im Bund für das Finanzierungsdilemma verantwortlich: "Man sieht eben, wie schwierig das ist, wenn man den Anfang einer Regierungszeit verstolpert. Das ist passiert", sagte der CDU-Politiker. Die großen Themen wie etwa die Deregulierung seien nicht angegangen worden - daher brauche man nun so viel Geld.
Kretschmer verwies auf die gemeinsame Forderung der Ministerpräsidenten nach günstigerem Strom. "Wir haben gesagt: Wenn wir wirtschaftliche Leistungsfähigkeit erhalten wollen, muss dieser Schritt kommen." Daher müsse man jetzt zum Beispiel über den Zertifikatehandel oder über die von Wirtschaftsministerin Katherina Reiche im sogenannten Netzpaket vorgeschlagenen Maßnahmen reden. Deutschland verliere sonst den Anschluss.
Dafür brauche es einen parteiübergreifenden Ansatz. "Jeder muss etwas geben." Aber jeder müsse dann auch etwas zurückbekommen. Die Bundesregierung täte gut daran, auf die Ländervertreter zu hören. "Wir haben in vielen Punkten immer wieder früher erkannt, was notwendig ist. Wir haben Recht behalten", so Kretschmer. Die Steuermehreinnahmen 2027 gäben Finanzminister Klingbeil auch den notwendigen Spielraum für die Senkung der Stromsteuer.
Bovenschulte will die Mineralölkonzerne zur Kasse bitten
Ganz anders sieht das Kretschmers Kollege Andreas Bovenschulte von der SPD. Der Bremer Bürgermeister will eine Senkung der Stromsteuer vor allem über eine Übergewinnsteuer für Mineralölkonzerne gegenfinanzieren - ein Vorhaben, das bei der Union nicht auf Gegenliebe stößt. Die Konzerne hätten in der Krise massive Gewinne in Milliardenhöhe abgeschöpft. "Lasst uns endlich denen in die Tasche greifen, die vorher den Bürgerinnen und Bürgern in die Tasche gegriffen haben", forderte Bovenschulte.
Zwar gebe es bislang dafür ohne die Union keine Mehrheit, räumte der SPD-Politiker ein. Aber er habe es noch nicht aufgegeben, die CDU von einer Übergewinnsteuer zu überzeugen. "Ich kann es nicht verstehen, warum sich die Union dieser vernünftigen Lösung versperrt." Zuletzt habe auch der Generalanwalt beim Europäischen Gerichtshof erklärt, dass er eine Übergewinnsteuer für zulässig halte, sagte Bovenschulte mit Blick auf juristische Bedenken in der Union.
Zudem reiche eine Entlastung beim Strompreis nicht aus, so der SPD-Politiker. "Wir brauchen eine Einkommenssteuerreform, die die kleinen und mittleren Einkommen entlastet." Zu einer vernünftigen Gegenfinanzierung gehöre auch, "dass diejenigen, die tatsächlich mehr leisten können, auch ihren Beitrag dazu leisten". Der Staat habe viele aktuell teure Aufgaben - da kann es nicht sein, "dass man immer nur die kleinen Leute auffordert, den Gürtel enger zu schnallen".

title: Загарбники просунулися на Донеччині та Запоріжжі — DeepState
content_c:
Загарбники просунулися на Донеччині та Запоріжжі — DeepState
Російські загарбники продовжують атакувати позиції Сил оборони.
Протягом минулої доби російські загарбники просунулися поблизу Костянтинівки, що у Донецькій області.
Про це йдеться у повідомленні DeepState.
Аналітики заявили, що також було зафіксовано просування загарбників в районі села Воздвижівка Гуляйпільського району Запорізької області.
«Ворог просунувся поблизу Пазено, Калеників та у Різниківці», — заявили у DeepState.
На інших ділянках фронту просування ворога або Сил оборони не зафіксовано.
Раніше повідомлялося, що попри постійні спроби просунутися до Добропілля, загарбники не можуть закріпитися в місті, оскільки українські підрозділи виявляють і знищують ворожі групи.
Ми раніше інформували, що Збройні сили України продовжують активну оборону та стримують просування російських військ на ключових напрямках.

title: Одна людина загинула, ще 6 постраждали внаслідок пожежі у житловій 6-поверхівці в Харкові
content_c:
У неділю ввечері сталася пожежа в житловій 6-поверхівці в Індустріальному районі Харкова.
"На пожежі одна людина загинула, ще 5 постраждали, також вогнеборці врятували вісім мешканців", – повідомляє пресслужба ГУ ДСНС у Харківській області.
На момент прибуття пожежно-рятувальних підрозділів горіли квартири на 5-му поверсі будинку. Вогонь охопив 20 кв. м. Через сильне задимлення пожежним довелося рятувати людей із задимленого під'їзду.
Причина виникнення пожежі встановлюється.
До гасіння вогню були залучені 30 рятувальників та 8 одиниць техніки ДСНС.
Джерело: https://t.me/DSNS_Kharkiv/26780

title: El Salvador president says bodies found in Haiti are not those of hostages
content_c:
El Salvador president says bodies found in Haiti are not those of hostages
- Published
Four bodies handed over to special forces on a mission to Haiti to recover Salvadoran hostages are "not our men", El Salvador's president has said.
Nayib Bukele said a nongovernmental organisation delivered the human remains to one of Haiti's airports claiming they were four El Salvadoran air technicians, but that one of the corpses was a child's and another was wearing a different country's army uniform.
He had dispatched a military contingent, reportedly of hundreds of soldiers, on Thursday after the four men vanished after being ambushed by "heavily armed criminal groups".
The hostages had been part of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), which is tasked with tackling worsening gang violence in Haiti.
The men had been travelling back to their camp in an armoured vehicle when they were attacked in an area of the Caribbean island nation controlled by armed groups called Croix-des-Bouquets. No gang has so far claimed responsibility.
Bukele previously said the Salvadoran military operation in Haiti had the sole purpose of returning the four men alive. Approximately 450 soldiers had so far been deployed, according to Haitian newspaper Le Nouvelliste.
Bukele said the bodies the mission had received included one of a man of "considerably greater height than that of our air technicians", a person "who was wearing part of a uniform from an army that is not ours", and that among the remains were identification cards and uniforms from other countries.
He posted pictures showing the ID card of a GSF member and a corresponding national ID card from Chad in Africa.
Bukele's comments poured skepticism on an earlier report in the New York Times, citing people close to the Salvadoran mission, that the bodies found on the outskirts of the Haitian capital, Port-au-Prince, on Saturday were thought to belong to the missing men.
The newspaper reported that the bodies delivered to the military contingent had been badly burned, meaning a medical examination would be required to identify them.
It cited one unnamed source briefed on the situation as saying the ID posted by Bukele in fact belonged to a soldier who had lost it when he had been injured.
Haiti has been ravaged by gang violence for years, but the situation has worsened in the political vacuum that followed the assassination of its president in 2021.
The multinational force dispatched to quell the violence and push back the armed gangs has struggled to penetrate areas where they hold sway.
More than 5,700 people have been killed or injured by gangs or during operations against them between 1 January and 11 September this year, the UN said at the start of October.
Bukele said the four GSF members had primarily been there to "carry out medical evacuations and save lives, not to wage war".
When they were abducted, helicopters were deployed and multiple attempts were made to reach the location, but these efforts were hampered by fighting in the area, the Salvadoran armed forces said.

title: Former RAAF pilot who allegedly murdered wife was ‘love rat’ and ‘master manipulator’, jury hears
content_c:
A former RAAF pilot was a “love rat” and “master manipulator” who staged his wife’s death to make it appear like an accident, a jury has heard.
Robert John Crawford, 49, pleaded not guilty on Monday to murdering his wife, Frances Elizabeth Crawford, at Upper Lockyer on 29 July 2024.
Her body was found near a ride-on lawnmower at the bottom of a retaining wall on their sprawling rural property west of Toowoomba.
Crawford murdered his wife in the context of a long relationship breakdown, prosecutor Chris Cook told a Brisbane supreme court jury.
The husband then embarked on a long campaign to make her death appear an accident, Cook alleged.
Four women with whom Crawford allegedly had affairs are due to be called as witnesses.
“He made out to be a man with good Christian values,” Cook said.
“However, his story did not match his behaviour. He was a man who lived a double life for a long time.”
Cook described Crawford as “a cheater, adulterer, love rat, philanderer and womaniser”.
The jury was told Crawford was not committed to the marriage, with the couple on the verge of divorce when the victim died.
The members were told Crawford was motivated to kill his wife because he stood to lose financially in a divorce settlement. He wanted to retain possession of the couple’s house and did not want to split his superannuation.
The jury was told Crawford wavered between divorcing her husband and giving him the chance to prove himself to her and their children. She had set her husband a detailed list of boundaries, including “deal breakers” that would lead to divorce.
The deal breakers included sexual or emotional infidelities, pornography and masturbation, the court was told.
Justice Lincoln Crowley told the jury the prosecution would allege Crawford caused his wife’s death either by strangulation or blunt-force trauma.
The jury will be taken to the site of the alleged murder on Wednesday.
Crowley told the jury the viewing would help them to understand the evidence.
The trial is expected to hear from up to 47 witnesses over the next three weeks.
Crawford’s defence barrister has not yet delivered an opening statement.

Rahul Gandhi targets BJP over alleged voter deletions, announces Delhi rally
Congress leader and Member of Parliament Rahul Gandhi on Sunday urged students, farmers, workers, women, young people and traders to join a "Save the Vote, Save the Country" march and rally in New Delhi on November 1.
The proposed rally, alleging widespread deletions from electoral rolls and violations of rules, is planned to be held at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan.
In a post on X, the opposition leader alleged votes were being "stolen" by the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
"Names have been removed from the voter lists. Rules and laws have been broken," Gandhi wrote, adding that people "will not tolerate this quietly" anymore.
Various organizations in India, including the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), are protesting a sweeping exercise which has so far purged over 130 million names from the country's draft electoral rolls.
